title: Accept https redirect URIs for dynamically registered clients
body:
Stacked on #2296 (base: `oauth`). First of three gap-closers taking the minimal OAuth 2.1 stack to connector grade.

Hosted MCP connectors register over DCR with https callback URLs, which the loopback-only policy rejected. [9f7fa82](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/9f7fa82122f2350df81f6c37a20d3964f0181f85) widens the registration policy:

* **Accepted**: http loopback URIs (unchanged, port-flexible matching) and https URIs on non-loopback hosts (exact matching, fragments rejected).
* **Still rejected**: plain http on public hosts, custom schemes, https on loopback hosts.
* Operator-provisioned clients are unaffected; the `trusted` flag stays manual provisioning only — dynamically registered https clients remain untrusted and go through the consent screen.

Model validation and the DCR endpoint enforce the same policy, with model and integration tests for both sides plus exact-match authorization behavior for https redirects.

Next in stack: refresh tokens + expiry, then confidential clients.

title: Expire OAuth access tokens and rotate refresh tokens
body:
Stacked on #3080. Second of three gap-closers for #2296.

The minimal stack issued non-expiring access tokens with no refresh path. [7041285](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/7041285c7b3ba5f06fc2655deffe6629b4a942b5) adds OAuth 2.1 token lifecycle:

* **OAuth-issued access tokens expire** an hour after issuance and carry a refresh token, both generated at creation. Personal access tokens are untouched: no expiry, no refresh token.
* **`refresh_token` grant with rotation semantics**: each refresh rotates both the access token and the refresh token on the grant record, so the previous refresh token dies with the rotation and Connected Apps still shows one grant per client. Refresh requests must present the `client_id` the grant was issued to.
* **Bearer authentication ignores expired tokens** (`Identity.find_by_permissable_access_token` goes through an `active` scope).
* **Revocation accepts either token** and kills the whole grant, per RFC 7009's "token" being either type.
* Discovery and DCR responses advertise the `refresh_token` grant.

Token responses now include `expires_in` and `refresh_token`; the refresh response omits `scope` (unchanged from the original grant, per RFC 6749 §6).

Deliberately not done: refresh-token reuse detection beyond rotation (a reused rotated token simply fails as unknown), and refresh-token expiry — grants live until revoked from Connected Apps, matching the existing revocation model.

**Update:** both are now done, stacked above #3082. #3160 adds replay detection: a rotated token presented again revokes the grant, except for a 60s retry grace. #3161 adds idle expiry: a grant lapses after 90 days without a refresh.

title: Support confidential clients with client_secret_post
body:
Stacked on the refresh-token PR. Third gap-closer for #2296, matching what beta2's bc3 authorization server advertises. Two conformance decisions also land here: **D3 (client_secret_basic)** and **D4 (revocation client authentication)**. This PR owns client authentication, and both decisions reverse lines that were in this body before. D1 and D2 are stacked above it in #3160 and #3161.

[1ca8787](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/1ca878765) adds confidential client support:

* Clients carry a `token_endpoint_auth_method` (`none`, `client_secret_post` or `client_secret_basic`). Confidential clients get a generated `client_secret` at creation. It is returned once in the DCR response, and `.compact` keeps it out of public-client responses.
* The token endpoint authenticates confidential clients on both grants. Public loopback clients are unchanged.
* Secrets are stored in plaintext and compared in constant time, the way the stack already stores access tokens.

### D3: client_secret_basic ([d65d011](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/d65d0117c))
RFC 6749 §2.3.1 says the server MUST support HTTP Basic for clients issued a password. This mirrors basecamp/bc3#13678 ([`Oauth::ClientAuthentication`](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/eaef1313ce322f1642f6619b042be74972a889a8/app/controllers/concerns/oauth/client_authentication.rb)).

* `Oauth::ClientAuthentication` reads either transport. It base64-decodes the Basic value strictly, splits on the **first** colon, and form-urldecodes each half (Appendix B), so `%3A` becomes `:` and `+` becomes a space ([bc3](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/eaef1313ce322f1642f6619b042be74972a889a8/app/controllers/concerns/oauth/client_authentication.rb#L193)). A confidential client's secret verifies whichever way it arrives, because the registered method is advisory.
* Ambiguity ([bc3](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/eaef1313ce322f1642f6619b042be74972a889a8/app/controllers/concerns/oauth/client_authentication.rb#L164)):

  | Request | Answer |
  |---|---|
  | Basic plus a non-empty body `client_secret` (even an identical one) | 400 `invalid_request`: more than one method (§2.3, §5.2) |
  | Basic plus a body `client_id` naming the same client, or an empty `client_secret=` | authenticates |
  | Basic plus a body `client_id` naming another client | 401 `invalid_client` |
  | Malformed Basic (bad base64, no colon, empty id, bad %-encoding, invalid UTF-8) | 401 `invalid_client` |
  | Basic naming a public client | 401 `invalid_client`: a public client holds no password |

* **`invalid_client` is 401 + `WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="<issuer>"` only for a failed Basic attempt, and 400 with no challenge for everything else** ([b6b8329](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/b6b83296a)). "Everything else" is a failed `client_secret_post`, a public client presenting a secret, a secret that authenticates no client, and a body failure beside an Authorization header of another scheme (which until now drew a Basic challenge). Why:
  - A bare 401 violates RFC 9110 §15.5.2, which requires a challenge.
  - A Basic challenge to a request that never tried Basic names a scheme that doesn't apply to it.
  - oauth4webapi and openid-client turn a challenged 401 into a `WWWAuthenticateChallengeError` instead of `invalid_client`.
  - A 401 + Basic on a form POST can pop a browser auth dialog.

  This is the policy settled across bc3, Fizzy and HEY after an adversarial review; it supersedes the earlier "every `invalid_client` is 401" ([9b27557](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/9b2755792)). Fizzy has no deployed clients, so nothing depends on the old status. Status, body and header remain identical for an unknown client and a wrong secret.
* The pilot gate keys on the Basic id. Discovery advertises `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported: [none, client_secret_post, client_secret_basic]`, and DCR accepts `client_secret_basic`. bc3 pins DCR to `none`, but Fizzy's DCR already accepted `client_secret_post`, so Basic joins it.

### D4: revocation client authentication ([e80b5b6](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/e80b5b615))
RFC 7009 §2.1: validate the client's credentials, then check that the token was issued to that client. This mirrors bc3's [`Oauth::RevocationsController`](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/controllers/oauth/revocations_controller.rb#L25-L65), and the Basic branch mirrors [#13678](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/eaef1313ce322f1642f6619b042be74972a889a8/app/controllers/oauth/revocations_controller.rb#L41).

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| Confidential client, correct secret (post or Basic), its own token | 200, grant revoked |
| Confidential client, missing or wrong secret in the body | 400 `invalid_client`, no challenge, nothing revoked |
| Any Basic header that doesn't authenticate (unknown id, wrong secret, public client) | 401 `invalid_client` + `WWW-Authenticate: Basic`, whatever the token |
| Public client naming its `client_id`, its own token | 200, grant revoked |
| Authenticated client presenting another client's token, an unknown token, or a PAT | 200, nothing revoked (§2.2) |
| No `client_id`, or an unknown one, without Basic or a client secret | 200, nothing revoked |
| A client secret that authenticates no client (no `client_id`, an unknown one, or a public client, which holds no password) | 400 `invalid_client` ([c9375f1](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/c9375f186), [29a5d11](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/29a5d118c)). bc3 answers 200 here; Fizzy treats any presented secret as an authentication attempt, as its token endpoint does |
| A personal access token, with no client credentials or with credentials that authenticate | 200, token revoked |
| A personal access token, with client credentials that fail to authenticate | `invalid_client` (401 + Basic if via Basic, else 400), nothing revoked |

The row for a missing or unknown `client_id` follows bc3. When no client is identified, the request has *failed to identify* a client rather than failed authentication, so it gets the non-oracular 200 and not `invalid_client`. **Personal access tokens stay revocable here** ([98619ab](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/98619ab8f), Jeremy's decision: revocation is uniform across token kinds, and PATs may later be rebuilt on OAuth, see #3164). A PAT has no client, so holding it is the credential. Client credentials presented alongside it must still pass the rules above. Discovery advertises `revocation_endpoint_auth_methods_supported: [none, client_secret_post, client_secret_basic]`.

The old line "Revocation stays unauthenticated by design" is withdrawn. Codex's [revocation thread](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/pull/3082#discussion_r4190956123) asked for exactly this change.

### Tests
`test/integration/oauth_client_secret_basic_test.rb` and `test/integration/oauth_revocation_test.rb` are new. I wrote them first: 20 failures and 1 error before the change, and the 3 that passed were guards for behavior that already existed. They cover Basic-only refresh and code exchange, `%3A`/`+` decoding, both-methods → 400, header/body id mismatch, five malformed shapes, Basic naming a public client, unknown client vs wrong secret giving identical answers, a post failure → 400 without the challenge (also beside an Authorization header of another scheme), the pilot gate reading the Basic id, a drift test (every advertised secret method authenticates), DCR, the revocation rows above, including the cross-client revoke, and personal-access-token revocation, which is possession-based but still refused on failed client authentication. A revoked PAT then stops authenticating. Existing tests expect 400 for a non-Basic `invalid_client` (written first: 17 failures before [b6b8329](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/b6b83296a)), and revocation requests in them name their `client_id`.

Locally: `bin/rails test test/integration test/models test/controllers` passes (1517 tests).












## Shipped-client matrix for the `invalid_client` 401 → 400 change

None of the OAuth endpoints are live yet, since this train is unmerged. No first-party Fizzy client calls `/oauth/token`, `/oauth/revocation` or any other `/oauth/*` or `/.well-known/oauth-*` path. I checked every tag and every remote branch.

| Client (shipped, min supported) | Auth today | Body-auth failure at token or revocation: 401 → 400 | Basic failure (unchanged, 401 + Basic) | Branches on 400 vs 401 at `/oauth/*` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fizzy-ios `v1.0-233`, no force-update | magic link, then the `session_token` cookie | not called, unaffected | not called | no |
| fizzy-android `1.1.3-14`, no force-update | magic link (`LoginApi.kt:31-56@1.1.3-14`), then the cookie | not called, unaffected | not called | no |
| fizzy-cli `v4.0.1` | Bearer PAT (`internal/client/client.go:238,648@v4.0.1`) | not called, unaffected | not called | no |
| fizzy-sdk `v0.2.4` | Bearer or cookie (`go/pkg/fizzy/auth_strategy.go:31,51`); its `AGENTS.md:60` says "no OAuth" | not called, unaffected | not called | no |
| fizzy-mcp-server, fizzy-popper (main, no releases) | Bearer PAT | not called, unaffected | not called | no |

The PAT and session flows don't touch these endpoints: PATs go only to API routes as Bearer, and sessions go to `/session*`. The Fizzy server has no minimum-version gate. The only OAuth-shaped client code was a HEY-copied `CalendarAccessTokenUpdater.swift` on the fizzy-ios `multi-identity-setup` branch. It never shipped, was removed in `6920f9f`, and treated 400 and 401 alike. The planned hosted-MCP exchange client (fizzy-mcp-server `docs/hosted-plan`) should expect a 400 `invalid_client` for a body-auth failure.

title: Trusted Types report-only pilot: 1% of SaaS page loads, collected first-party
body:
## Trusted Types report-only pilot: 1% of SaaS page loads, collected first-party

Track 2 of the [Security Hardening card](https://app.basecamp.com/2914079/buckets/48540453/card_tables/cards/10239442945)'s Trusted Types work, **stacked on #3194** (track 1: the same inventory from system tests, no production data). #3194 covers the paths our system tests visit. This covers the ones real use reaches.

**Waits on the Trust & Compliance card:** https://app.basecamp.com/2914079/buckets/48697456/card_tables/cards/10411063168. Don't merge before it's answered.

### What changes

- **Sampling.** `TrustedTypesReportOnly` (from #3194) sends `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` on a share of HTML responses. The share comes from `CSP_TRUSTED_TYPES_SAMPLE_RATE` or `config.x.content_security_policy.trusted_types_sample_rate`. Unset or 0 means off. Anything outside 0..1, or not a number, fails at boot, so a `1` meant as "1%" can't become 100% silently past 1. A document keeps the policy it loaded with across Turbo Drive visits, so this samples page loads, and a sampled page reports until it's reloaded.
- **SaaS production turns it on at 1%** ([`saas/config/environments/production.rb`](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/ad6f0696bd82412995a04eb5a0f163ab62fac336/saas/config/environments/production.rb)), with `report-uri /trusted_types_reports`. Staging and beta inherit it. OSS installs get nothing unless they set the rate.
- **A first-party collector instead of Sentry.**
  - [`TrustedTypesReportsController`](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/ad6f0696bd82412995a04eb5a0f163ab62fac336/app/controllers/trusted_types_reports_controller.rb) is unauthenticated, account-less, skips CSRF, reads at most 16 KB and allows 120 reports a minute per IP.
  - [`TrustedTypesViolation`](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/ad6f0696bd82412995a04eb5a0f163ab62fac336/app/models/trusted_types_violation.rb) logs one line per report, for example `Trusted Types violation: sink=Element innerHTML source=/assets/lexxy-….js:8063:17 route=cards#show`.
  - It drops the content sample, the page URL, the query string and everything else in the report. Other directives, malformed bodies and mistyped fields are accepted and ignored, without raising.
- **The route only accepts `application/csp-report`**, which is what browsers send to `report-uri`. Rails parses an `application/json` body into params and logs it in "Parameters:" before any controller code runs. That case was verified to leak the sample into the log, and now gets a 404.

### Why not Sentry, as the first version of this PR did

Every Trusted Types report carries `sink|first 40 characters written`, and that can be what a person typed. Codex reproduced lexxy editor text in it. Nothing on our side can stop that before Sentry:

| | Chrome 155 | Firefox 150 (Playwright build) | WebKit 26.4 (Playwright build) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sample in the `securitypolicyviolation` event | yes | yes | yes |
| Sample in the `report-uri` POST | yes | yes | no (WebKit's report-uri serializer omits `script-sample` for every type; `report-to` includes it) |
| Changed by adding or omitting `'report-sample'` | no | no | no |

- The spec builds the sample unconditionally ([Trusted Types §4.2.4](https://w3c.github.io/trusted-types/dist/spec/#should-block-sink-type-mismatch)). `'report-sample'` only governs inline and eval violations ([CSP3 §4.2.3](https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-csp/#should-block-inline), [§4.4.1](https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-csp/#can-compile-strings)).
- **Sentry can't scrub it either.** Relay marks `csp.script_sample` as non-PII, so no Advanced Data Scrubbing selector matches it. Tested against `sentry-relay` 0.10.1 with synthetic events: `csp.script_sample` is accepted and changes nothing, while `csp.source_file` was redacted.
- On top of that, `fizzy-csp` has IP scrubbing off and a key with no rate limit.

So this is the one design that keeps the sample out of a third party: the sample never leaves Fizzy.

Not verified: real Safari (safaridriver timed out creating a session), stock Firefox (Playwright's patched build was used), and Sentry's hosted Relay (local bindings and current source only).

### Evidence

- Focused tests: 17 runs, 0 failures (`trusted_types_violation_test`, `trusted_types_reports_controller_test`, `trusted_types_report_only_test`, `static_csp_test`). These include an injected newline in the sink, a query on the script URL, and non-integer line and column numbers.
- Mutation check: making the controller also log the raw body fails the "without the content" test.
- **End to end on thelio** (scratch `report_uri` in test.rb, not committed). Real Chrome on a card page plus a Drive visit sent **46 reports**, which logged 19 distinct sink/source/route lines. **0 occurrences** of the synthetic content anywhere in `log/test.log`.
- Rate parsing: `0` leaves the middleware out, `0.01` gives 0.01, `1` gives 1.0. `1.5`, `-1`, `1e309` and `abc` each raise at boot.
- Production volume: about 619k requests a day (7-day average of `rails_request_total`), and about 15 reports per sampled editor page. At 1% that's at most around 90k report requests a day, likely well under, since most requests aren't full page loads. Each one is a 204 with a log line.

### Risk and rollback

- **Blocks nothing.** It's report-only, on its own header, and the enforcing policy is byte for byte unchanged.
- **Turn it off:** `CSP_TRUSTED_TYPES_SAMPLE_RATE=0` and redeploy. Pages already open keep reporting until they're reloaded, and the collector keeps accepting until reverted.
- **New unauthenticated POST endpoint.** It's capped by size and rate. The worst abuse is extra fixed-shape log lines: sink, path and route are reduced to `[\w ]` and `[\w/.-]` and length-capped.
- **Request metadata is logged like any request.** The report POST's `Referer` is the reporting page's full URL, query included. Rails structured logging records it, and so would a Sentry exception report. Declined (codex round 2, P1): it's the same URL Fizzy logged when it served that page, to the same logs and the same Sentry. Browsers set it, and nothing here adds to it.
- **Declined (codex round 2, P2): malformed `application/json` posts.** With detailed exception pages off, the 404 path tries to parse the body and logs the raw text on a parse error. Browsers never send that type to `report-uri`, so the only bytes that can reach the log are the poster's own. Every route has that property.
- **Declined (codex round 2, P2): the rate limit doesn't stop logging or cache work.** A request over the limit still costs one log line and one Solid Cache increment, like any request to any route. Body-size and slow-body limits belong at the proxy, not in this controller. To end the pilot, set the rate to 0. Pages already open keep reporting until reloaded, and that tail is a bounded number of fixed-shape log lines.
- **Declined (codex round 1, P2): caching correlates sampling.** Public boards (`max-age=30`), 304 revalidation and the service worker's offline copy can replay a sampled policy, or withhold one. That skews which documents report. Now that a report carries no content, it can't widen exposure. It isn't worth making documents uncached for.

### Owner steps outside the repo

- **None for this design.** Reports don't touch Sentry.
- **Separately, for `fizzy-csp`** (Sentry project owner, team `sip`): consider turning on "Prevent storing of IP addresses" and setting a rate limit on its key. That's for the existing CSP reports, not this PR.

### The decision this feeds, and who reads it

- **Decision:** the enforcement design. It needs the list of sinks to migrate onto a single named `createHTML` policy, and the policy hooks Turbo and lexxy need before `require-trusted-types-for` can enforce.
- **Reader:** TBD (operator to fill in).
- **Review date:** TBD (operator to fill in). That's when to read the collected lines and set the rate back to 0.

title: Give the load balancer the real client IP
body:
Fixes [Fizzy: !o 4xx fizzy returns internal IPs, not public IPs](https://app.basecamp.com/2914079/buckets/21350690/card_tables/cards/9850708467).

## The bug

Cloudflare puts the caller's address in `True-Client-IP`. For most of our apps the F5's `manage_x_forwarded` iRule copies that into `X-Forwarded-For`, but fizzy's HTTPS virtual server is `fastL4` passthrough, so no HTTP iRule can run. kamal-proxy only ever knew about `X-Forwarded-For` and the TCP peer, so the app tier's access log — the `web-*` index the `!o 4xx` report reads — records an internal address. Rails escaped this because `TrackTrueClientIp` does the copy itself before `ActionDispatch::RemoteIp`.

## The change

kamal-proxy 0.10.0 added `--client-ip-header` (Kevin's [#224](https://github.com/basecamp/kamal-proxy/pull/224) work), which makes the proxy trust a named header both for its own access log and for the `X-Forwarded-For` it sends on. So, at fizzy-lb:

- `--client-ip-header=True-Client-IP` in `saas/script/configure-lb-*.sh`.
- `--forward-headers` alongside it. Without this the rewrite only fixes the LB's own log: `X-Forwarded-For` is dropped by default when the proxy terminates TLS, which it does here, so the app tier would keep seeing the peer address. kamal-proxy's own test for the flag pairs the two the same way.
- The LB accessory image moves from `basecamp/kamal-proxy:lb` to `basecamp/kamal-proxy:v0.10.2`. Required, not cosmetic — the `lb` tag was built in Nov 2025 and would reject `--client-ip-header` outright. v0.10.2 over v0.10.0 for its fixes: AEAD-only TLS 1.2 ciphers, client timeouts on the public listeners, path-prefix matching on the cleaned path. Pinning also stops what a host runs depending on when it last rebooted, same reasoning as hotcell's image in `deploy.yml`.
- `saas/script/configure-lb-mcp.sh` (the hosted Fizzy MCP's route, added since this PR opened) already passes both flags and refuses a balancer whose kamal-proxy lacks `--client-ip-header`. Its comment now says that guard only fires on a balancer not yet rebooted onto the pin. The hosted MCP keys its per-user rate limits on the client address, so it can't be routed until this rolls out.

`TrackTrueClientIp` stays. The card thread suggested it becomes deletable, and it does become redundant for traffic through the LB, but it still covers the app when reached directly and it collapses the forwarded chain to the one address we trust. Worth removing separately, once this is live.

## Worth a look before rolling out

- **The app tier's `remote_addr` becomes a list**, `"<public>, <lb peer>"`, because `SetXForwarded` always appends the peer. The public address is first, but if `client.ip` is mapped as an ES `ip` field, a two-element string may fail to index — check the report and the mapping before running the production script. A single clean value at the app tier needs Kamal to expose `client_ip_header` for the managed proxy; 2.12.0 doesn't, so the app-tier proxy stays on Kamal's default `v0.9.2` for now.
- **No new trust.** `--client-ip-header` means anything reaching the LB with a `True-Client-IP` header sets its own logged address — but `TrackTrueClientIp` already trusts that header unconditionally today, so this places no trust we weren't already placing.
- **The `lb` tag's provenance isn't recorded anywhere.** Every flag the configure scripts pass (`--read-target`, `--writer-affinity-timeout`, `--tls-acme-cache-path`) exists in v0.10.2, and v0.10.2 ignores the old build's extra keys in its saved state, and the one unmerged load-balancer branch adds `X-Kamal-Writer`, which fizzy doesn't reference. Still worth staging first.

## Rollout

Config changes only, no app deploy. Neither change takes effect on its own: the image needs an accessory reboot, and the new flags need the configure script re-run afterwards (routes come back from saved state, but without the new flags).

1. **Staging, then beta1, then production.** Check the access log and the `!o 4xx` report on each before moving on.
2. **One balancer at a time,** so each datacenter's pair always has one serving: `bin/kamal accessory reboot load-balancer -d <destination> --hosts <one balancer>`, then that destination's `saas/script/configure-lb-<destination>.sh`, then confirm `https://<app host>/up` before the next balancer.
3. **Then the MCP route,** per destination: `saas/script/configure-lb-mcp.sh <destination>`.

**Rollback:** re-pin `basecamp/kamal-proxy:lb`, reboot the balancer, and re-run the configure script without the two new flags.

## Testing

`bin/ci` green locally (every step; `gh signoff` only wanted the branch pushed) on the original head; GitHub CI on the updated head.

title: Answer API authentication failures with a Bearer challenge
body:
Stacked on #3082 (train: #2296 → #3080 → #3081 → #3082 → this → #3160 → …; #3160 was restacked onto this on 2026-10-17, so the line is linear). The gap predates the train, but #3081's hourly expiry makes it load-bearing, so it rides on the tip.

### Problem
Every bearer failure got Rails' default `WWW-Authenticate: Token realm="Application"`, with no error code. JSON requests that sent no credentials were redirected to the sign-in page. RFC 6750 §3 says challenges MUST use the `Bearer` scheme, including when credentials are missing. A read-only token used on a write got the same 401 as a dead token. An OAuth client would then refresh, get another read token (a refresh can't widen scope), and loop.

### Change
| Request | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Unknown, expired, revoked or dark-server OAuth token | 401 `Token realm` | 401 `Bearer … error="invalid_token"` |
| Valid read-only OAuth grant, non-GET/HEAD | 401 `Token realm` | 403 `Bearer … error="insufficient_scope", scope="write"` |
| Valid read-only personal access token, non-GET/HEAD | 401 `Token realm` | 401 `Bearer … error="insufficient_scope", scope="write"` (status unchanged for shipped clients) |
| JSON, no credentials | 302 to sign-in | 302, unchanged (see D6 below) |
| Bearer header on an HTML request | 401 `Token realm` | 401 `Bearer … error="invalid_request"` |
| `bearer <token>` (lowercase) | 302 to sign-in | authenticates (RFC 9110 §11.1) |
| `Basic …Bearer…` | treated as bearer | not bearer |

- `resource_metadata` (RFC 9728 §5.1) is built from the same `root_url(script_name: nil)` as the metadata's `resource`. It is included only while `Oauth::Availability.acceptance_enabled?`, so a dark server never points at a URL that 404s.
- `Identity.find_by_permissable_access_token` is replaced by `Identity::AccessToken.find_honored`, which leaves the method check to the controller. That way a dead token and a token with too little scope get different answers. Expiry and the availability gate still come first: an expired read token on a write is `invalid_token`, not `insufficient_scope`.
- The scheme gate parses the scheme with the same `AUTH_SCHEME_REGEX` Rails uses, so the gate and the parser agree. When DPoP lands, it widens this predicate.

### D6: shipped clients keep their answers (decided 2026-10-17)
The native apps and fizzy-cli rely on two of the old answers, and #3191 pins both: a read-only personal access token writing gets 401, and a JSON request with no credentials gets a 302 to sign in. So only an OAuth grant gets the 403. A credential-less JSON request keeps the 302, because nothing in it tells a shipped client from an OAuth one. That 302 is a recorded deviation from RFC 6750 §3 (rubric DS-3; `docs/oauth/spec_conformance.md`, `docs/oauth.md` on #3193). Hosted OAuth clients discover Fizzy's authorization server through fizzy-mcp-server's own 401 + `resource_metadata` and Fizzy's `/.well-known` metadata, so the deviation costs them little. **Exit:** once the oldest supported native app and fizzy-cli handle a 401 challenge there. It also keeps `@rails/request.js` (card autosave) and the direct uploader on the redirect they handle.

### Unchanged
- Personal access tokens stay identity-wide and never expire.
- Non-JSON requests are still refused for bearer auth, except on ActiveStorage, where bearer auth is allowed as before.
- Session-cookie JSON still works, because `resume_session` runs first.
- The `require_account` redirect for untenanted paths is untouched.

### Tests
`test/controllers/api_test.rb` asserts the status and exact challenge for each row above. It also checks that the advertised `resource_metadata` URL resolves to metadata whose `resource` is the root URL, and that the parameter is absent while OAuth is dark. A read-only OAuth grant's write gets 403; a read-only personal access token's write keeps its 401 with the `insufficient_scope` challenge; a credential-less JSON request is redirected. #3191's pins pass unchanged on the train. API docs: `docs/api/README.md`.

title: Sweep self-registered OAuth clients left without a grant for 30 days
body:
Stacked on #3161 (`oauth-grant-idle-expiry`): #2296 → #3080 → #3081 → #3082 → #3160 → #3161 → **#3159** → #3163. It moved there from #3082 on 2026-10-06 so that its overlap with #3160 and #3161 (the tokens controller, `Identity::AccessToken` associations and grant destruction) is settled in this PR instead of at merge time. See the restack comment for details.

Client registration is open and unauthenticated. Its only brake is 10 registrations per minute per IP. Nothing ever deletes an `oauth_clients` row, so abandoned registrations only accumulate, and MCP clients often re-register on every install or reconnect (RFC 7591 §5 asks the server to mitigate this). bc3's `Oauth::CleanupJob#cleanup_unused_dcr_clients` sweeps never-authorized DCR clients after 30 days. This PR adds the same sweep to Fizzy.

### What changes
- **Daily sweep:** `config/recurring.yml` runs `Oauth::Client.cleanup` every day at 04:12. It destroys dynamically registered clients that hold no access token and have had no grant activity for `UNUSED_RETENTION` (30 days). Operator-provisioned clients (`dynamically_registered: false`) are never swept.
- **The clock starts at the last grant, not at registration:** a grant touches its client after it is created or destroyed (`after_commit`, not `belongs_to touch: true`, so no transaction holds a grant while waiting on its client, which used to deadlock against a replayed code exchange). Consent touches the client too, so a client isn't swept while its 60-second code is live. Fizzy has no record of whether a client was ever authorized. Without the touch, an app registered 60 days ago that the user disconnected yesterday in Connected Apps would be swept tonight. On reconnect it would then hit "Unknown client" at authorize. Refresh rotation uses `update_all` and doesn't touch, so steady use adds no writes.
- **The sweep and issuance share one lock:** `destroy_if_still_unused` locks the client row and reruns the full stale test (tokens and timestamp) before destroying it, like bc3's `obliterate_if_still_unauthorized`. The code exchange now issues through `Oauth::Client#redeem`, which takes the same row lock. There's no foreign key to stop it, so before this a token could commit between the sweep's recheck and its delete. Now the grant either lands before the recheck, which then spares the client, or finds the client already gone and gets `invalid_grant` "Unknown client". Codex caught this in review, and it was fixed in fa904e5e3.
- **`has_many :access_tokens, dependent: :destroy`:** a manual client `destroy` can't strand tokens, and each grant's own cascade runs, so retired refresh tokens from #3160 go with it.
- **Missing client rows:** the refresh grant now answers a token whose client row is gone (for example after a manual `delete`) with `invalid_grant` instead of `NoMethodError` (a 500). The code grant already answered a missing client with `invalid_grant`.

### Tests
- On #3161: when idle expiry deletes a lapsed grant, the deletion touches the client too, so the client gets a full 30 days before this sweep removes it ("Pin that a grant swept for lapsing restarts its client's retention period"). Removing `touch: true` makes this test fail.
I wrote the tests first and watched each one fail before its change. I mutation-checked three mechanisms, and each mutation fails its test:
- removing `touch: true`
- making the recheck unconditional
- issuing without the row lock

The race test deletes the client between the exchange reading it and issuing the token.

The full OSS SQLite suite passes locally: 1802 tests, 0 failures, 1 skip. Rubocop is clean.

### Fixed underneath, in #2296 ("Point a client's access_tokens at oauth_client_id, and drop the stray foreign key", now 65e4d3e7c)
- **`Oauth::Client#access_tokens` was broken:** it inferred `client_id` as the foreign key, a column `identity_access_tokens` doesn't have. Nothing used the association until this sweep.
- **Stray foreign key in `db/schema.rb`:** it declared `add_foreign_key "identity_access_tokens", "oauth_clients"`, but the AddOauth migration says `foreign_key: false` and `db/schema_sqlite.rb` has no such key. So databases built by running migrations had no foreign key, while MySQL databases loaded from the schema (CI and fresh installs) had one.

### Not done, on purpose
- **RFC 7592 management, initial access tokens, host vetting:** the hosted plan keeps registration open for Cursor-style clients. Host vetting belongs with CIMD in phase C.
- **Global registration cap:** one actor's abuse would become a registration outage for every legitimate client.
- **24-hour retention:** a client can register and authorize days later from a cached client_id. 30 days matches bc3.

### Behaviour to know
- A self-registered client whose user disconnected it and that then sees no new grant for 30 days is swept. If the app comes back with its cached client_id it gets "Unknown client" and has to register again. bc3 sweeps on "never authorized", and Fizzy can only approximate that with "no grant activity for 30 days".





**invalid_client status policy:** the conformance record now reflects #3082 `b6b83296a`. A failed Basic attempt gets 401 + Basic; any other `invalid_client` gets 400. The shipped-client matrix is in #3082: no first-party Fizzy client calls `/oauth/*`.

title: Revoke the grant when a rotated refresh token is replayed, with a 60s retry grace
body:
Stacked on #3082 (train: #2296 → #3080 → #3081 → #3082 → this → #3161 → #3159 → #3163). Implements **D1: refresh replay detection** of the Fizzy OAuth conformance decisions. It is a new PR, not a commit on #3081, because #3081 is converged and adding to it would mean rebasing #3082, #3158 and #3159. The "Deliberately not done: refresh-token reuse detection" line in #3081's body is superseded by this PR.

### Problem
Since #3081, each refresh rotates the grant's refresh token in place, and the old token is forgotten. A rotated token that came back failed as unknown with `invalid_grant`. Nothing else happened. If an attacker stole a refresh token and refreshed first, the attacker owned the grant. The legitimate client's next refresh failed quietly, and nothing revoked the thief's copy. OAuth 2.1 §4.3.1 and RFC 9700 §4.14.2 call for rotation *with* replay detection: a rotated token presented again means two parties hold the grant, so the server revokes it.

### Change ([1b0c206](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/1b0c20662), then [677752a](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/677752a78) and [e783576](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/e78357692); [49ba964](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/49ba96436) locks the grant before its retired tokens are deleted, so destroy and rotation take locks in the same order). Each retired row records the successor its rotation issued. A retry is answerable only while that successor is still the grant's current refresh token, judged against a single read of the grant, so the check depends neither on clock order nor on a second query.
Each rotation retires the presented token into `oauth_retired_refresh_tokens`. A retired token presented by the grant's own client is answered as follows:

| When | Answer | bc3 |
|---|---|---|
| Within 60s of its rotation, and the successor it produced is still current | 200 with **that same successor pair** (same access token, same refresh token). Nothing rotates. | [`rotate!` grace branch](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/models/oauth/refresh_token/rotation.rb#L72-L80), [`within_grace_window?`](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/models/oauth/refresh_token/rotation.rb#L35-L42) |
| Within 60s, but the successor has itself rotated | `invalid_grant` "Refresh token superseded", no revocation. The client demonstrably holds the live descendant. | [`successor_for_retry!`](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/models/oauth/refresh_token/rotation.rb#L214-L215) |
| 60s or more after its rotation, any ancestor | Grant revoked, successor included; `invalid_grant` | [`revoke_family!(reason: "refresh_reuse")`](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/models/oauth/refresh_token/rotation.rb#L78) |
| A refresh that loses a concurrent rotation | Answered as a grace retry, so it gets the winner's successor | [lost-race branch](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/models/oauth/refresh_token/rotation.rb#L90-L91) |
| Presented under another client's `client_id` | `invalid_grant` as before, no revocation. The destructive branch is reachable only by the grant's own client. | [`find_presented!` checks the client before rotation](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/models/oauth/refresh_token.rb#L140-L150) |

- **The window is 60s, and it is a constant.** bc3's per-client `refresh_replay_grace` [defaults to 60](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/db/schema.rb#L1257) ([README](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/doc/oauth/README.md#L977)). Fizzy has no per-client TTL columns, so it uses that default. The boundary matches bc3's strict `rotated_at > grace.ago` ([L38](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/models/oauth/refresh_token/rotation.rb#L38)): 59s retries, and exactly 60s revokes.
- **The replay is judged before the requested scope.** Otherwise a replay asking for a scope outside the grant would get `invalid_scope` and skip the revocation.
- **Revocation (RFC 7009):** presenting a rotated refresh token at `/oauth/revocation` revokes its grant, as bc3's revocation of any family member does. The ownership check from #3082 still applies.
- **Retention:** retired tokens are swept daily after 90 days (`Oauth::RetiredRefreshToken.cleanup` in `config/recurring.yml`). That matches bc3's [90-day `refresh_token_ttl`](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/models/oauth/first_party_clients.rb#L51), after which a rotated bc3 token has expired too. Revoking a grant deletes its retired tokens.

### Accepted trade-off (same as bc3)
For 60s after a rotation, anyone holding the just-rotated token who can name the client gets the successor pair back. For a public client, naming the client takes only its `client_id`. This is the cost of the grace window D1 asks for: without it, a client that lost a response would be revoked as a thief. Once the window closes, the same presentation revokes the grant.

### Tests (written first; 6 of 10 integration tests failed before the change, and the other 4 guard against over-revoking)
- `test/integration/oauth_refresh_replay_test.rb`: same successor at 59s, revoke at exactly 60s, revoke after a day, an older ancestor revokes, superseded refused without revoking, another client's replay doesn't revoke, a lost race serves the winner, an out-of-grant scope still revokes, and revoking through a rotated token works but only for its client.
- Also: a successor rotated by a host whose clock runs behind still supersedes the retry, and a grant deleted mid-request answers `invalid_grant`, not a 500.
- `test/models/oauth/retired_refresh_token_test.rb`: rotation retires the token, the race loser retires nothing and the winner's successor stays retryable, revocation deletes retired tokens, and cleanup respects retention.
- Mutation checks: `>=` at the boundary fails the 60s test, a window 2s shorter fails the 59s test, dropping `!superseded?` fails the superseded test, and removing the scope guard fails the scope test.
- `oauth_flow_test` "refresh grant invalidates the previous refresh token" now replays after the grace window.

Locally: `bin/rails test test/integration test/models test/controllers` passes on SQLite (1531 tests). The MySQL `schema.rb` entry was written by hand to match the dumper's sorted format, and CI's MySQL jobs load it.

title: Lapse OAuth grants left idle for 90 days
body:
Stacked on #3160 (train: #2296 → #3080 → #3081 → #3082 → #3160 → this → #3159 → #3163). Implements **D2: idle expiry** of the Fizzy OAuth conformance decisions. It is a new PR for the same reason as #3160: #3081 owns expiry but is converged, and reopening it would rebase the train. The "Deliberately not done: refresh-token expiry" line in #3081's body is superseded here.

### Problem
A Fizzy OAuth grant lived until someone revoked it. A refresh token left in an abandoned client stayed good forever.

### What bc3 does
bc3 has no separate idle timer. Every rotation mints a refresh token with `expires_at: client.refresh_token_ttl.seconds.from_now` ([refresh_token.rb L80](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/models/oauth/refresh_token.rb#L80), [L113](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/models/oauth/refresh_token.rb#L113)), and the TTL is [90 days](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/models/oauth/first_party_clients.rb#L51). So "idle" means **no refresh for 90 days**, and every refresh restarts the clock. Using an access token doesn't extend anything. A token is expired once [`expires_at < Time.current`](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/models/oauth/refresh_token.rb#L211-L212), and the token endpoint then refuses it with `invalid_grant` ([L148](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/models/oauth/refresh_token.rb#L148)).

### Change ([3c78975](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/3c789754d), [21f8ada](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/21f8adae3), [8aafeae](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/8aafeae3e), [cf33269](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/commit/cf33269f3))
- **The idle clock is the grant's `updated_at`.** Only issuance and rotation write a grant, and every rotation sets `updated_at`, including rotations by code from before this PR. A grant lapses once `updated_at + 90 days` (`Identity::AccessToken::REFRESH_IDLE_LIMIT`) has passed. The first version stored a `refresh_token_expires_at` column. Codex found two ways it could fall out of step during a rolling deploy: a NULL written by old code, and a stale backfilled deadline left behind when old code rotated. 8aafeae dropped the column, so there is no migration. The trade-off: any future code that writes to a grant row also restarts its idle clock, and the constant's comment says so.
- A refresh on a lapsed grant answers `invalid_grant` "Refresh token expired". The client has to restart authorization, and the user re-consents, since Fizzy's consent screen always shows. This check runs after the client check and does not apply to rotated tokens. Those still go through #3160's replay handling, so a replay of a lapsed grant's old token revokes it, as bc3's [rotated-and-expired branch](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/models/oauth/refresh_token.rb#L148) does.
- Rotation itself matches only unlapsed grants, so a refresh already in flight can't renew a grant past its deadline. The sweep also locks and rechecks each grant before deleting it, so a grant renewed after selection is spared, even one renewed by pre-idle-expiry code mid-deploy.
- Lapsed grants drop out of Connected Apps and out of the profile page's entry point. A daily sweep (`Identity::AccessToken.cleanup`, `config/recurring.yml`) deletes them along with their retired tokens. bc3 keeps expired refresh rows 7 more days for debugging ([cleanup_job.rb](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/146d02715eb1c0836d0c9017979647367791508f/app/jobs/oauth/cleanup_job.rb#L26)). Fizzy has no audit consumer for them, so it deletes them at once.
- `Oauth::RetiredRefreshToken::RETENTION` now references the same limit.

### Tests (written first; each failed before the change it pins)
`test/integration/oauth_grant_idle_expiry_test.rb`:
- a refresh at exactly 90 days works, and one at 90 days + 1s lapses as `invalid_grant`
- a refresh at day 89 restarts the clock, so day 178 still refreshes
- a lapsed grant leaves Connected Apps
- the sweep deletes lapsed grants and keeps live grants and PATs
- rotation refuses a grant that is already past its deadline
- the sweep spares a grant renewed after it was selected
- a rotation by older code (which writes only the token and `updated_at`) restarts the clock
- the profile page's Connected Apps link disappears once every grant has lapsed

Mutation check: removing the `unlapsed` filter from the profile page fails its test.

The tests move the clock with `travel_to Time.current + d`, not `travel d`. `travel` adds calendar days in the machine's local zone, so across a DST change it lands an hour off the model's UTC arithmetic. That flipped the exact-boundary test locally.

Locally: `bin/rails test test/integration test/models test/controllers` passes on SQLite (1540 tests). This PR makes no schema change.

title: Prefix newly issued access tokens, refresh tokens and personal access tokens
body:
Stacked on #3159, the tip of the OAuth train (#2296 → #3080 → #3081 → #3082 → #3160 → #3161 → #3159).

New tokens now start with a prefix that says what kind of token they are:

| Kind | Prefix |
|---|---|
| Personal access token | `fizzy_pat_` |
| OAuth access token | `fizzy_at_` |
| OAuth refresh token | `fizzy_rt_` |

With a prefix, a person, a log scrubber or a secret scanner can tell a Fizzy credential on sight, and which kind it is. The random part is 44 base58 characters (the alphabet `has_secure_token` uses, drawn through Ruby's `SecureRandom.alphanumeric`), 257 bits, at least bc3's 32 bytes (rubric TK-1). It was 24 characters, about 140 bits, until 2026-10-17; credentials issued earlier keep working, since lookups match the whole string.

**Existing tokens keep working.** Tokens issued before this change have no prefix. Every lookup still matches the whole string: Bearer authentication, refresh, revocation and replay detection. A grant issued before this gets prefixed tokens the next time it rotates. A personal access token keeps the token it was issued with until someone revokes it.

### How Basecamp and HEY do it

- **Basecamp (bc3)** defines its prefixes in `Oauth::TokenGenerator::PREFIXES` (`app/models/oauth/token_generator.rb`):
  - `bc_at_` for access tokens, including personal access tokens, which are OAuth access tokens issued by the `bc-personal-access` client
  - `bc_rt_` refresh tokens, `bc_code_` authorization codes, `bc_dc_` device codes
  - `bc_cs_` client secrets, but only the ones issued by its rake task (agent client secrets are unprefixed `base58(43)`)
  - `bc_iat_` initial access tokens

  The random part is `SecureRandom.hex(32)` with no checksum, and bc3 stores HMAC digests rather than the raw tokens. It routes requests by prefix: `bc_at_` goes to bc3's own OAuth tokens and anything else to the legacy Launchpad tokens.
- **HEY (haystack)** doesn't use prefixes. Its OAuth access and refresh tokens are signed `MessageVerifier` payloads, and its client uid and secret are plain `has_secure_token` values.
- **Secret scanning:** neither app is registered with GitHub's secret-scanning partner program. Neither repo has an alert endpoint or a pattern file for one.

Fizzy uses a separate `fizzy_pat_` prefix for personal access tokens, unlike bc3. That keeps the kind visible on sight, and it stays meaningful if personal access tokens are later rebuilt on OAuth (see #3164).

### GitHub secret-scanning partner registration: worth pursuing later, not now

- **What it would buy:** GitHub would notify us when a Fizzy token is pushed to a public repo, and push protection could block the push in the first place. The likeliest leaks are personal access tokens pasted into fizzy-cli or MCP configs. #3082 makes personal access tokens revocable by whoever holds one, so an alert handler could revoke a leaked token immediately.
- **What it would cost:**
  - A public endpoint that verifies GitHub's signed alert payloads
  - A pattern for GitHub to register
  - Ongoing ownership of both
- **Caveats:**
  - Self-hosted Fizzy issues the same prefixes, so some alerts would be for tokens we never issued. The handler would just find nothing, but it adds noise.
  - There's no checksum, so GitHub can't rule out false positives offline. A CRC suffix, as GitHub's own tokens have, would fix that. It would be a format change to make before registering.
- **Recommendation:** worth pursuing once OAuth is out of the dark and personal access token use grows. It isn't pursued here.

### Not in this PR

Client secrets carry `fizzy_cs_` too (added 2026-10-17 for rubric TK-1, as bc3's rake-issued secrets carry `bc_cs_`), drawn by the same generator: `Identity::AccessToken.generate_token(:client_secret)`.

### Tests

- `Identity::AccessTokenTest`: each kind gets its prefix and the base58 body. A grant issued before prefixes rotates into prefixed tokens.
- `OauthFlowTest`: the code exchange returns prefixed tokens. An unprefixed grant still authenticates against the API and refreshes into prefixed tokens. An unprefixed personal access token still authenticates.
- `OauthRevocationTest`: unprefixed personal and OAuth tokens still revoke.

title: Add support for single sign-on (SSO) through OIDC IdP
body: This PR adds the ability for Fizzy to sign people in through one OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider for the whole server. When SSO is configured, it will become the only way to log in to Fizzy. (Magic links, passkeys, auto-login links, signups by email, join links, and personal access tokens will stop working.) Here are a couple of screenshots showing some of the UI additions (Figure 1, 4, and 6) when SSO is configured: _Figure 1: Fizzy login screen when SSO is configured_ _Figure 2: IdP (Keycloak) login screen_ _Figure 3: Choosing accounts (from an admin's perspective)_ _Figure 4: The account settings page (from an admin's perspective)_ _Figure 5: Choosing accounts (from a regular user's perspective)_ _Figure 6: Being denied access to an account due to the IdP user not belonging to the group assigned to the account_ This work added one new table, `identity_single_sign_on_links`, which has six columns: `id`, `identity_id`, `issuer`, `subject`, `created_at`, and `updated_at`. It also has two unique indexes, one on `[identity_id, issuer]` and one on `[issuer, subject]`. It also adds three columns to existing tables: - `sessions.single_sign_on_authenticated_at` of type `datetime`: The time when the session last signed in through SSO - `sessions.single_sign_on_groups` of type `text`: The session's groups (as JSON) - `accounts.single_sign_on_group` of type `string`: The account's group path. Account access and admin privileges for each of the users are configured through groups in the IdP. The account `Honcho` can be assigned the group `/fizzy/engineers`, which will make only the members of `/fizzy/engineers` able to access that account. Users under the group defined in `SINGLE_SIGN_ON_ADMIN_GROUP` will have admin privilege for every account. They will also have the ability to create new accounts. Please refer to the SSO documentation under [`/docs/single-sign-on.md`](https://github.com/gjazali/fizzy/blob/main/docs/single-sign-on.md) to learn more about the features added here, their behaviors, their configuration parameters, and their effects. I tested this out using Keycloak as the IdP.

title: End an app's own plumbing with its grant; keep what it set up for the account
body: Resolves the two open #2296 threads on [webhook credentials](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/pull/2296#discussion_r4195098392) and [push subscriptions](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/pull/2296#discussion_r4198379156). An OAuth grant is a delegate: someone the user handed authority to. What a delegate sets up comes in two kinds, and until now the model couldn't tell them apart: - **The app's own plumbing ends with the app.** A push subscription registered through a grant delivers to the app's own device or install. It now records its OAuth client ([`Push::Subscription#oauth_client`](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/ec809fecd779ebe4c228373651cb0559aba706a1/app/models/push/subscription.rb#L13-L17)), and it's destroyed when the identity's last grant to that client ends. - **What a delegate set up for the account survives, attributed and visible.** A webhook a grant creates is an account resource. If you told an agent to wire up webhooks for your account, losing them when you disconnect it would be a nasty surprise. A webhook now records its creator and the app it came through. The board's webhook settings show "Created by via ", and the webhook outlives the grant. - **The person decides at revoke time.** The Connected Apps disconnect confirmation lists the webhooks the app set up for you, with an **Also remove** option, off by default. Choosing it removes exactly the webhooks it listed, along with the grant. ## Placement This is stacked on the train's tip (#3163), not folded into a train PR. The hook has to cover idle lapse (#3161) and replay revoke (#3160), so it belongs above both. No train PR above those owns push subscriptions or webhooks. ## The single point where grants end Every way a grant ends destroys its `Identity::AccessToken` row: Connected Apps disconnect (`destroy_all`), RFC 7009 revocation, the idle-lapse sweep, a replayed refresh token, a replayed authorization code, and the client's `dependent: :destroy`. So the hook is an `after_destroy_commit` on the grant ([`end_app_plumbing`](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/ec809fecd779ebe4c228373651cb0559aba706a1/app/models/identity/access_token.rb#L54-L64), [body](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/ec809fecd779ebe4c228373651cb0559aba706a1/app/models/identity/access_token.rb#L147-L151))). It deletes the client's push subscriptions for the identity's users once no grant to that client remains. It runs after commit, so if two grants to one client end at once, whichever commits second sees none left. Running inside the transaction, each would still see the other's uncommitted row and skip the delete. A process killed between commit and callback leaves its subscriptions behind, and the delivery gate below makes them inert. **Delivery is the guarantee; the hook is cleanup.** The hook finds subscriptions through the user's *current* identity, so it can't see any way the user and the grant part first: the user leaving the account, moving to another identity after an email change, or a registration landing just after the last grant ended. Review found these one at a time, so rather than patch each path, an app's subscription now delivers only while the user's identity holds an **unlapsed** grant to that app ([`Push::Subscription.deliverable_to`](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/ec809fecd779ebe4c228373651cb0559aba706a1/app/models/push/subscription.rb#L19-L28), used by [`Notification::PushTarget::Web`](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/ec809fecd779ebe4c228373651cb0559aba706a1/app/models/notification/push_target/web.rb#L10)). Anything the cleanup misses is inert. The gate also closes the window between a grant lapsing and the daily sweep. A re-registered endpoint goes to whoever registered it last, so an app that registers a fresh client on reconnect keeps its device subscription. ## Revoke-time removal is scoped twice [`Webhook.set_up_through(client, identity:)`](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/ec809fecd779ebe4c228373651cb0559aba706a1/app/models/webhook.rb#L43-L47) limits removal to webhooks created through that client by one of this identity's users, in accounts where that user is still an active admin (the same bar `WebhooksController` sets). The posted `webhook_ids` are then intersected with that set. Posting another person's webhook, another app's, or a hand-made one removes nothing, and a webhook the app created after the dialog was drawn stays. Webhooks are removed before the grant goes, so if a removal fails, the app is still listed and you can try again. ## Account transfer The export carries every webhook column, and the import refuses any `belongs_to` that points at an existing record. Exported, `created_via_id` (an instance-global OAuth client) would fail the import wherever that client exists. It's now left out of the webhook record set, and `creator_id` is declared optional, so an export from an instance on an older version (no attribution columns) still imports ([manifest](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/ec809fecd779ebe4c228373651cb0559aba706a1/app/models/account/data_transfer/manifest.rb#L37-L40)). `creator_id` travels, since the creator is a user in the export. This was found by a failing-first test, now in the second commit. ## Tests [`oauth_delegate_resources_test.rb`](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/ec809fecd779ebe4c228373651cb0559aba706a1/test/integration/oauth_delegate_resources_test.rb), written first; 14 of its first 16 tests failed before the change, and each test added for a review finding failed before its fix. With the delivery line reverted, the four delivery tests fail. The two that passed already are regression guards: another client's revocation, and disconnecting without also-remove. - A grant-created push subscription records its client and is removed on **disconnect**, **revocation**, **idle lapse** and **replay revoke**. It survives while another grant to the same client remains. - **Delivery** includes an app's subscription only while its grant is live. Delivery stops when the user leaves the account, moves to another identity, or the grant lapses (before the sweep), and when a subscription is claimed for an app with no grant left. The browser's subscriptions keep delivering. A **re-registered endpoint** moves to its latest registrant. - **Session-** and **PAT-created** push subscriptions record no client and survive. - A grant-created webhook records creator and app, **survives disconnect**, and shows its attribution on the show and index pages. - **Also remove** removes exactly the listed webhooks of that app for this person, in active accounts only. Another app's, another person's, a hand-made one, a forged id and one added after the dialog was drawn all stay. - **Another client's revocation** leaves this client's push subscriptions and webhooks alone. - The account round trip keeps a webhook's creator and drops its app, and an export made before this change still imports ([`import_test.rb`](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/ec809fecd779ebe4c228373651cb0559aba706a1/test/models/account/import_test.rb)). Locally: the full SQLite suite passes (2011 tests), RuboCop and Brakeman are clean, and a real disconnect with "Also remove" checked in the browser removed only that app's two webhooks. ## Screenshots | | Light | Dark | |---|---|---| | Disconnect confirmation | | | | Board webhooks | | | | Webhook | | | (The images live on the `pr-assets/oauth-delegate-resources` branch, pinned to its commit. The secret shown is from a local seed database.) ## Decided against, or deferred - **App-owned event subscriptions** (Fizzy's counterpart to bc3's `Mcp::EventSubscription`) are not built. They're the right home for apps that need events for their own operation. Tracked in #3168. - **The person column is `creator`, not `created_by`**, to match `Board`, `Card`, `Comment` and `Filter`. The app column is `created_via`. It's attribution, so it's named differently from the push subscription's `oauth_client`, which is ownership. - **A swept client.** A self-registered client with no grants is swept after 30 days. Its webhooks then read "via an app that's since been removed" rather than losing the attribution. - **The webhook JSON doesn't expose attribution.** Nothing asked for it, and it can be added later.
