title: Keep beta1's staff-only OAuth and MCP exchange setup on main
body:
Brings beta1's staff-only OAuth setup from the 2026-10-24 integration branch onto `main`, so a beta1 deploy from `main` keeps it. It's two cherry-picked commits.

- **beta1 web env:** `OAUTH_ACCEPTANCE_ENABLED`, `OAUTH_CIMD_ENABLED`, and `FIZZY_OAUTH_MCP_RESOURCES` pointing at beta1's MCP server. These sit in the `@beta_number == "1"` block, next to the existing `OAUTH_STAFF_ONLY: "true"`. OAuth on beta1 stays limited to 37signals staff.
- **beta1's `fizzy_mcp` accessory:** the token-exchange URL, and the exchange client `fizzy-mcp-server-beta1`. beta1 shares production's database, so its MCP server gets a client row of its own. The secret is fetched in `secrets.beta`.

The integration branch's non-migrating beta `cmd` is deliberately left out, so beta boots on `main` as usual. After this, the only differences between `main` and the integration branch are `main`'s newer lockfiles and that `cmd`.

Verified by rendering beta1's Kamal config: web env names only, the web `cmd` unset, and the accessory's exchange env and secret name. No secret values were read.

### Third-party data flow

This adds no new third party and no new kind of data. A 37signals staff member (`OAUTH_STAFF_ONLY`) can connect an OAuth app of their own choosing, such as Claude or ChatGPT, to beta1. The data that reaches that app is what they authorize, for the scopes they grant. The existing Trust & Compliance card for people connecting third-party apps already covers that flow; this is the same flow the OAuth train already ships, here limited to staff on beta1. Client ID Metadata Documents are fetched anonymously from the allowlisted hosts in `deploy.yml` and carry no personal data.

The `fizzy-mcp-server-beta1` exchange client is ours, so it is not a third party. It has been provisioned with its own secret.

title: Upgrade rails to 83ddc9f6
body:
Fizzy's Rails pin, `4658033f`, is 626 commits behind rails/rails main. This moves it to `83ddc9f6`, today's tip of main, in both `Gemfile.lock` and `Gemfile.saas.lock`. Only the Rails revision line changes in each: no gemspec in the range changes a dependency, so no other gem moves, and `bin/bundle-drift` is clean.

None of the 626 commits needs a code change in Fizzy. One is worth watching after deploy. Rails used to move an `INDEX(...)` hint from a count's subquery to the outer `COUNT`, where MySQL ignored it; now it stays in the subquery and takes effect (`d6a7aac0`). `Filter#cards` (`app/models/filter.rb:75`) applies `use_index(:index_cards_on_account_id_and_last_active_at_and_status)` and geared_pagination counts it as `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT …)`, so the filtered card count now uses that index. EXPLAIN that count on staging for a board-filtered card list and watch the slow-query log after deploy; if the hint hurts the count, `unscope(:optimizer_hints)` before counting.

Collection rendering was rebuilt in this range (`51da0298`) and broke Jbuilder collections until `a909b38e` and `33fc52d0`; Fizzy jumps from before the change to after both fixes. A quick look at a few `.json` collection endpoints on staging is cheap insurance.

`ColumnPaginationRefreshTest#test_a_broadcast_refresh_keeps_every_page_of_a_column` fails intermittently in the SaaS system suite. It is not from this bump: across the same 10 seeds it failed 4 of 10 times on `56b534b14` (this PR's base) and 4 of 10 on this branch, always with 15 of 18 cards. The test's scroll to "load more" races the expander's select-and-scroll of the first card (`navigable_list_controller.js:119-121`), and when the selection scrolls last, page 2 never loads.

Full plan: [`upgrade-analysis/fizzy-20261027-rails_4658033f..83ddc9f6.md`](https://github.com/basecamp/37signals-hq/blob/b228646b/upgrade-analysis/fizzy-20261027-rails_4658033f..83ddc9f6.md), also posted below as a comment.

title: Converge Fizzy's first-party OAuth clients from one registry
body:
Adds `Oauth::FirstPartyClients`, a registry of the OAuth clients Fizzy ships with, modelled on bc3's. Before this, each client was made its own way: a migration and a first-use fallback for the personal access issuer, and `oauth:provision_mcp_client` for each MCP server. Each wrote its own subset of attributes.

## What it does
- **Definitions:**
  - `fizzy-personal-access`, the personal access token issuer.
  - The hosted MCP servers, by the resource each fronts: `fizzy-mcp-server` for `https://mcp.fizzy.do/mcp`, and `fizzy-mcp-server-beta1` for `https://beta1-mcp.fizzy-beta.com/mcp`.
- **A total BASELINE.** Each definition merges over every policy column `oauth_clients` has, so a converge resets drift in anything a definition doesn't name. A test pins the baseline to the table's columns, so a new column must be added to it.
- **One transaction.** Every client converges, or none does.
- **No secret is ever minted or rotated.** A confidential client's live secret survives a converge. A new confidential client is created with no secret at all, so any client without one, never minted or since cleared, is named in the task output on every run until `oauth:mint_client_secret` gives it one. A public row loses any stray secret.
- **No client is turned back on.** Fizzy has no disabled flag. A hosted MCP client is turned off by clearing its secret, which no converge writes back, or by dropping its resource from `FIZZY_OAUTH_MCP_RESOURCES`, which takes the client out of the converge altogether.
- **No repointing.** An MCP client is refused rather than moved when it fronts a resource that's still configured, as before, or a hosted resource. A hosted resource is configured only on its own destination, so its row isn't safe to move from any of them.
- **One entry point for operators and seeds.** `bin/rails oauth:provision_first_party_clients` runs it, and so do the development seeds. `Oauth::Client.personal_access_issuer` takes its attributes from the registry, so the issuer made on first use matches what a converge writes.

## Design choices
- **Hosted MCP clients are scoped by `FIZZY_OAUTH_MCP_RESOURCES`.** The resource URLs are literals in the registry, but each one converges only where `FIZZY_OAUTH_MCP_RESOURCES` names its resource. That's the only place its client can exchange tokens (`Oauth::Client#delegation_client?`).
  - Production and the betas share a database. Under this scoping, production's converge never writes beta1's row, and beta1's never writes production's.
  - Development and self-hosted installs serve neither resource, so they get neither client.
  - The alternative was to converge every literal everywhere, as bc3's registry does. That creates beta rows from a production console, and production's row on every install.
- **`oauth:provision_mcp_client` stays, as a thin wrapper.** It's still the way to provision an MCP server the registry doesn't host, such as a self-hosted install's own. The registry can't name those, and retiring the task would leave them no way in. It now converges through the same `converge!` and BASELINE as everything else, so its rows reset drift too. A hosted resource and its client can't be provisioned apart, which closes a hole: a shared database could otherwise have hosted rows repointed from a destination where their resource isn't configured. `Oauth::Client.provision_mcp_client!` moves into the registry as `provision_mcp_server!`.
- **`oauth:mint_client_secret` is unchanged.**
- **Staging is not in the registry.** `deploy.staging.yml` names a staging MCP resource but no exchange client, and staging sets no `FIZZY_OAUTH_MCP_RESOURCES`. It can be added when staging is lit.

## Tests
`test/models/oauth/first_party_clients_test.rb` and a task test. Each guarantee was checked by breaking it and watching its test fail:

| Break | Test that fails |
|---|---|
| touch every row on converge | converging again changes nothing |
| merge without BASELINE, or without part of it | drift in any baseline attribute is reset |
| let BASELINE's nil `client_secret_digest` through on confidential rows | a live secret survives a converge |
| mint a secret for a confidential row that has none | a client turned off by clearing its secret stays off |
| converge every hosted definition regardless of configuration | a production converge creates no beta client; a client turned off by dropping its resource stays off; an install that serves no hosted MCP resource gets no MCP client |
| drop the transaction | a converge that fails partway writes nothing |

title: Stop hover and column expand from scrolling the board to the last hovered card
body:
On a board with a long, paginated Maybe column, hovering a card or clicking a column's expander scrolled the board down to the last hovered Maybe card, pushing the column headings out of reach. It shows up sharply on Windows with animations off, where there's no transition to blend the extra scroll into. Basecamp card: https://3.basecamp.com/2914079/buckets/27/card_tables/cards/10450239847 (Fizzy #3184, originally reported in #1746's area).

The cause is in `navigable-list`: `selectItem` scrolled its target into view and let `focus()` scroll again on top, and that fired for every `mouseenter` and for every expander click, where the outer board list's `selectCurrentOrReset` cascades into the nested column list and re-selects its remembered card.

This builds on #3037 by @gitKashish, kept as the first commit with their authorship: auto-scroll becomes an opt-in of `#setCurrentFrom`, hover and `selectCurrentOrReset` skip it, `focus()` always gets `preventScroll: true`, and card hotkeys scroll explicitly after a triage. On top of that:

- Arrow-key moves between columns and restored selections scroll the selected card into view again, which #3037 had dropped.
- Tabbing into a column still scrolls its remembered card into view (`:focus-visible`), while clicking the column does not.
- A system test pins all of it: expander clicks and hovers leave the board where it is, clicking a column's empty space focuses the remembered card without scrolling, and Shift+Tab into the column scrolls it into view. The test fails on main and passes here.

Supersedes #3037. Still needs a check on an affected Windows 10 machine (Chrome/Edge, animations off) before the card is closed.

title: Pin fizzy-mcp-server v0.2.1
body: Moves the `fizzy_mcp` accessory image from v0.2.0 to v0.2.1 (`sha256:fc63d6b2…a428a`). v0.2.1 adds `FIZZY_MCP_UPSTREAM`; with it unset, v0.2.1 behaves as v0.2.0. App deploys do not reboot the accessory.

title: Sweep dynamic registrations nobody authorized after a day
body:
Answers the dynamic-registration volume finding on #3247 ([thread](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/pull/3247#discussion_r4408148087)).

`POST /oauth/clients` is unauthenticated and limited to 10 a minute per address. Each registration can hold ten 2,000-character redirect URIs, and a registration nobody authorized was kept for `UNUSED_RETENTION`, 30 days. This shortens that one case to 24 hours, so the rows such registrations can pile up are bounded by the registration rate over a day rather than a month.

## What counts as never authorized

`Oauth::Client.never_authorized`: a dynamically registered client whose `updated_at` still equals its `created_at`, and which holds no access token (`stale` keeps its `where.missing(:access_tokens)`). Nothing has touched the row since registration wrote it. The code already touches a client:

- when the user approves consent, before the code is issued (`Oauth::AuthorizationsController#create`);
- when a grant is created or destroyed (`Identity::AccessToken#touch_oauth_client`).

So a client that ever got a code or a grant, including one whose grant has since been revoked or lapsed, has `updated_at > created_at` and keeps the 30-day rule counted from its last grant activity, as before. Denying consent touches nothing, so a denied registration lapses after a day too.

If some future write updates a dynamically registered client, it moves `updated_at`, so the client falls back to 30 days. That errs toward keeping rows, never toward deleting one.

## What's untouched

- **Metadata document (CIMD) clients** were already swept after 30 days unused, and still are. They aren't created through `POST /oauth/clients`, so they keep 30 days.
- **Trusted, first-party and operator-provisioned clients** (`dynamically_registered: false`) were never swept and still aren't. That includes the personal access issuer.
- The lock-and-recheck in `destroy_if_still_unused` re-runs the whole `stale` test, so a consent or grant that lands between picking a client and destroying it still spares it.

## Schedule

`cleanup_oauth_clients` moves from daily (04:12) to hourly (minute 14), so a never-authorized registration lives at most about 25 hours. The sweep scans `oauth_clients`, which this change keeps small.

## Accepted loss

If someone registers and is still on the consent screen when the registration turns 24 hours old, their approval gets "Unknown client". MCP clients register again on reconnect, so the cost is one retry.

## Not doing: an account-wide or global registration budget

A global cap swaps a storage problem for an availability one. Someone registering from many addresses could use it up, and then real Claude or Cursor users couldn't register at all, which is worse than some extra rows. With the per-address limit and a one-day life, the row count is already bounded by the request rate, and the rows are small and grant nothing without a user's consent.

## Tests

- A never-authorized registration 25 hours old is swept, and one 23 hours old is kept.
- After a day, these are all kept: a registration with a live grant, one whose grant came and went, and one with approved consent.
- After a day, these unauthorized clients are all kept: trusted, operator-provisioned, metadata document, the trusted fixture and the personal access issuer.
- Integration: approving consent takes a 25-hour-old registration out of `stale`.
- One existing test changed. Its "recent" client registered 29 days ago and was never touched, so the new rule now sweeps it. It now registers 30 days ago and gets touched 29 days ago.

Each new test was checked by breaking what it covers: dropping the `updated_at = created_at` test, dropping the `dynamically_registered` restriction, setting the retention to 30 days, setting it to 22 hours, and dropping `where.missing(:access_tokens)`. Each break made at least one test fail. The OAuth model and integration tests pass on SQLite and MySQL 8.4. Nothing tests the hourly schedule.

title: Read the MCP container's configured image in mcp-rolling-reboot
body:
`saas/bin/mcp-rolling-reboot` checks that each host's `fizzy_mcp` container runs the configured image by comparing it with `docker ps --format '{{.Image}}'`. The image is pinned as `tag@sha256:digest` (#3254), and `docker ps` shows only the tag for a container started that way. So the check failed on a correct container, and the walk stopped with the first host still out of the load balancers.

This reads `docker inspect --format '{{if .State.Running}}{{.Config.Image}}{{end}}'` instead. That's the exact reference the container was started from, and it's empty unless the container is running. A missing container fails `inspect`, which reads as "nothing", so the walk stops as before.

**Tested:** the fixed script rolled production's `fizzy_mcp` through both hosts. The new check returned the full pinned reference on each host, and both are back in the load balancers. `bash -n` and `shellcheck` pass.

title: Admit directory reviewers through the staff-only OAuth gate, one identity per partner
body:
Held: don't merge or deploy without Jeremy's word.

## Why

Production OAuth runs with `OAUTH_STAFF_ONLY=true` until the consent screen and Connected Apps get design review. Directory reviewers (Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI/Cursor, Meta) still have to connect their apps to list Fizzy. Making a reviewer staff isn't an option, because staff also opens `/admin` and Mission Control.

Today reviewer sign-in has one shared identity, and its rotation sign-out destroys every token on that identity, OAuth grants included. On Basecamp, a shared reviewer login's Disconnect ended ChatGPT's daily scan. So each partner gets its own reviewer identity and code (and a scheduled scanner gets one of its own), and signing a reviewer out leaves its connected apps connected.

## What changed

**Core: a seam in the staff gate** (`app/models/oauth/availability.rb`)
- `Oauth::Availability.admit_beyond_staff(predicate)` registers a predicate on the identity. `admits?` asks it only when `staff_only` is on and the identity isn't staff. The predicate must return exactly `true`. Fizzy itself registers none, so OSS keeps admitting staff only.
- `Identity::AccessToken#honored_identity?` called `identity.staff?` directly, bypassing `admits?`. It now goes through `admits?`, so a reviewer's bearer token and refresh are honored too, and stop working once the reviewer is taken off the list. Every other staff-only call site (consent, code redemption, refresh, push subscriptions) already went through `admits?`.

**SaaS: reviewers pass the gate** (`saas/lib/fizzy/saas/engine.rb`)
- In `to_prepare`, the engine registers `Identity::ReviewerSignIn.method(:reviewer?)`. Only configured reviewer addresses pass. They are still not staff, so `/admin` stays closed (tested).

**SaaS: one identity and code per partner** (`saas/app/models/identity/reviewer_sign_in.rb`)
- New `FIZZY_REVIEWER_SIGN_IN_CODES` holds `email=sha256hexdigest` pairs, separated by commas or spaces. Each address signs in only with its own code.
- The existing `FIZZY_REVIEWER_SIGN_IN_EMAIL` / `FIZZY_REVIEWER_SIGN_IN_CODE_DIGEST` pair keeps working beside the list. Where both name an address, the list wins.
- An address listed with an empty digest (`email=`) is still a reviewer: it keeps the email and membership locks, the gate exemption and sign-out, but no code signs it in. That replaces "clear the digest" from the single-pair setup.
- Matching compares the presented address and code against every reviewer's entry with `secure_compare`, and doesn't stop at the first mismatch.

**SaaS: sign-out scope**
- Browser sign-out (`DELETE /session`) already ended only that browser's session and never touched tokens. It's now tested for a reviewer.
- `saas:reviewer_sign_in:sign_out` used to destroy every access token on the identity. That came from cbcf432a1 ("so a code holder can't keep a way back in"): it stopped someone holding the code from minting a token during a review and keeping it after rotation. It now removes **personal access tokens only**. Sessions, passkeys, transfers, join codes and Action Cable connections are handled as before, and **OAuth grants are left alone**.
- To keep a guard against a code holder's leftover app, `sign_out` now also lists every app connected as each reviewer (client name, client_id, connected at), next to the existing member list. Removing grants is a separate, explicit task: `saas:reviewer_sign_in:revoke_grants EMAIL=…`. It needs a reviewer named, and it never touches other reviewers or non-reviewers.
- `sign_out` takes an optional `EMAIL=` so one partner's rotation doesn't sign the others out. Without it, it covers every reviewer, as before.

**Rake**
- `saas:reviewer_sign_in:generate EMAIL=new-reviewer@example.com` prints the code and a complete `FIZZY_REVIEWER_SIGN_IN_CODES=` line: the existing entries (single pair included) plus the new one, or with that reviewer's digest replaced. Without `EMAIL=` it prints the single-pair digest line, as before.

## Production config change at deploy

Nothing is required: the existing single pair keeps working unchanged. To add per-partner reviewers:

1. Create one reviewer identity per partner (and one for a scheduled scanner), each in its own comped internal account.
2. For each one, run `bin/rails saas:reviewer_sign_in:generate EMAIL=<that reviewer's address>` and keep the code with the other reviewer credentials. Each run prints the cumulative line, so the last run's `FIZZY_REVIEWER_SIGN_IN_CODES=` line has every reviewer in it.
3. Add `FIZZY_REVIEWER_SIGN_IN_CODES` as a new production secret with that value. Wire it into the production deploy's secret env list and the secrets fetch, beside the two existing reviewer variables. This PR deliberately leaves that wiring out: fetching a secret that doesn't exist yet would fail the deploy.
4. Once the list carries the original reviewer too, the two single-pair variables can be removed (optional).

## Tests

- `test/models/oauth/availability_test.rb`: an extension's predicate admits under staff-only. Staff still pass, and others and `nil` are refused. A truthy non-`true` answer doesn't admit.
- `saas/test/integration/oauth_reviewer_staff_only_test.rb`, with a non-staff reviewer:
  - passes `admits?`, sees the consent screen and gets a code;
  - has its bearer token honored and its refresh accepted, until it's taken off the list;
  - is still refused `/admin`;
  - passes with an empty digest;
  - a non-staff non-reviewer is still refused at consent and on bearer use, and staff still pass.
- `saas/test/models/identity/reviewer_sign_in_test.rb`:
  - each listed reviewer signs in with its own code and not another's;
  - the single pair works beside the list, and the list wins where both name an address;
  - every reviewer's pair is compared with `secure_compare` (4 comparisons for 2 reviewers on a wrong code);
  - an empty-digest entry is a reviewer that no code signs in;
  - `sign_out` leaves OAuth grants and removes personal tokens;
  - `sign_out EMAIL=` scopes to that reviewer, and does nothing for a non-reviewer;
  - `revoke_grants` needs a reviewer named and touches only that reviewer's grants;
  - grant listing and the cumulative config line.
  - All existing tests (wrong code refused, other identity refused, blank input, unconfigured) still pass.
- `saas/test/controllers/sessions/reviewer_sign_in_test.rb`: two listed reviewers through the real sign-in flow; a reviewer's browser sign-out ends that session only and leaves the grant and the other browser's session.

title: Admit the connector platforms' OAuth requests as they send them
body:
Held: don't merge without Jeremy's word.

Three OAuth findings that block the directory listings of the hosted MCP server: Claude, ChatGPT, Grok/Cursor and Muse. The fourth, "creates that notify", is in basecamp/fizzy-mcp-server#21 and needed no change.

## `offline_access`

Claude, Cursor and Muse send `offline_access` beside the scopes they want. Basecamp's own records show Claude asking for `full read mcp offline_access`, Cursor asking for it at registration, and Muse's partner client configured with it. Consent answered `invalid_scope` to `read write offline_access`, because `Oauth::Client#allows_scope?` refused any scope the client didn't hold. A refresh naming it was refused the same way.

The scope only asks for a refresh token, and every grant Fizzy issues has one anyway. So consent and refresh now weigh a request without it (`Oauth.requested_scopes`), the way bc3 accepts and drops it (`Oauth::Scope::REFRESH_ONLY_SCOPES`). Alone, it still asks for nothing (`invalid_scope`), which matches what Client ID Metadata Documents already do (`scope: "offline_access"` is invalid there). The grant and the token response carry `read` or `read write` as before. Registration (DCR and CIMD) already dropped unknown scopes, so it's unchanged.

## Token rate limits

`/oauth/token` held code and refresh grants to 20 a minute per address. Every Claude.ai user redeems and refreshes from Anthropic's egress, and every ChatGPT user from OpenAI's, so one platform's traffic used up the budget of everyone behind it.

Each grant now gets its own limiter wherever the request names one. This follows the shape `Oauth::TokenExchangesController` already uses, and bc3's charge-to-the-client refund (`charge_authenticated_client!`). The rule is in `grant_rate_limit_key`:

| The request | Charged to |
|---|---|
| A code issued to the client presenting it | `code/<client>/<person>`, 20 a minute |
| A refresh token, live or rotated, of a grant issued to the client presenting it | `grant/<grant>`, 20 a minute |
| Anything else: an unknown token, another client's grant, a confidential client that fails to authenticate, Basic beside a body secret | The address, 20 a minute, as before |

Before any of that, a coarse ceiling of 3,000 requests a minute per address is charged for every request. Naming a grant costs a client lookup, a digest and up to two indexed reads, so past the ceiling a flood is refused before that work. One platform's egress sends far less than that.

A client "presents" a grant only when it authenticates, or when it's a public client presenting no secret. A stale or replayed refresh token is charged to its own grant, so a dead token spends only its own lineage's budget. That's bc3#13466's outage, where stale tokens' `invalid_grant`s from one egress blocked everyone behind it.

Choosing the limiter decides nothing about the request: the callbacks after it judge the code or token exactly as before. A code is checked by decryption alone. A refresh token takes the digest lookup that `set_refreshable_access_token` repeats from the query cache.

Not changed: revocation (`Oauth::RevocationsController`) is still 20 a minute per address. A platform revokes only when someone disconnects, but it's the same shape, if you want it keyed too.

## Muse

Basecamp took two routes for Muse (basecamp-mcp-server's `docs/listings/muse.md`). Custom connectors register by DCR from `muse.ai` and `agent.meta.ai`, admitted in bc3#13677 and in use. The listing has a partner confidential client, `muse-by-meta`, provisioned but untested, since Muse's review queue hasn't reached it. This PR mirrors the route shown working: `muse.ai` and `agent.meta.ai` join `OAUTH_DCR_ALLOWED_HTTPS_HOSTS`. Those are the hosts of Muse's three known callbacks:

- `https://muse.ai/connect/oauth-callback`
- `https://muse.ai/api/hatch/oauth/callback`
- `https://agent.meta.ai/api/hatch/oauth/callback`

A `muse-by-meta` slot in `Oauth::FirstPartyClients` waits until Muse's portal asks for client credentials.

**Third parties and personal data:** Muse is a new destination for customer data, sent at the customer's own direction, as with Claude and ChatGPT: Meta receives what a person asks Muse to fetch. Basecamp treats Meta as an independent controller under the Muse Connector Terms, not as a subprocessor. Per this repo's AGENTS.md, this needs a Trust & Compliance card before it ships.

## Tests

`test/integration/oauth_platform_clients_test.rb` covers:

- consent and a refresh with `offline_access`, and `offline_access` alone;
- a refresh, a rotated token's replay and a code going through while the address bucket is full;
- a grant's own budget refusing it;
- each kind of request that names no grant of its own staying on the address bucket.

`Oauth::Client#allows_scope?` gains cases. Without this change, the offline_access tests fail on `invalid_scope`, and the grant-limiter tests fail on 429 or on its absence.

## Release

Deploy Fizzy. The DCR hosts are in `saas/config/deploy.yml`'s env, so they take effect with that deploy.

title: Redesign the OAuth consent, Connected apps and error screens
body:
Held: don't merge without Jeremy's word.

## For design review

@jzimdars, this puts every OAuth screen in front of you in one sitting, with no live apps to set up.

**Run it.** In development, after `bin/rails db:seed`:

```sh
script/dev/oauth_states
```

It seeds the demo apps, grants and webhooks, then prints a URL or click path for every state, and the line to start the server with:

```sh
FIZZY_OAUTH_MCP_RESOURCES=http://app.fizzy.localhost:3006/mcp FIZZY_REVIEWER_SIGN_IN_EMAIL=… FIZZY_REVIEWER_SIGN_IN_CODE_DIGEST=… bin/dev
```

The MCP resource turns on the account picker. The reviewer variables turn on the fixed reviewer code, and they only work in SaaS mode. To sign in, enter one of the printed emails; development shows the code on the page. You can run the script again at any time, and it puts back anything you disconnected. `--print` reprints the directory, `--reset` removes the demo apps, and `--list` lists the states.

**What it prints, by screen.**

- **Consent** (as `david@example.com`)
  - a self-registered web app, with the "We haven't checked this app" warning
  - an app on your device, by loopback and by app scheme
  - an app named by a metadata document ("Name set by the app at claude.ai")
  - an app made by 37signals
  - a read-only request, with both options offered and Read only preselected
  - a read-only app, with a single option
  - many accounts, with the picker
  - one account, named with no picker (as `devoauth-one@example.com`)
  - a long name, a right-to-left name, and a right-to-left name on a self-registered app
- **Connected apps**
  - empty (`devoauth-empty`)
  - one app (`devoauth-one`)
  - many apps across all three groups, long and right-to-left names among them (`david`)
  - the disconnect dialog with no webhooks (Board Sync), one (Acme CLI), and several, one of them in another account (Demo Assistant)
  - the notice after disconnecting
  - the profile entry (`david`), and the profile with no entry before a first grant (`devoauth-empty`)
- **Error page**, one URL per code
  - `invalid_request`: unknown app, unregistered callback, and no PKCE challenge
  - `unsupported_response_type`, `invalid_scope`, `invalid_target`, `unauthorized_client`
  - `invalid_client_metadata`, which needs a network connection
  - `access_denied` (as `devoauth-no-account`)
  - `temporarily_unavailable` and `slow_down` have no URL. They use the same page with their own sentence.
- **Server postures**, one restart each
  - staff only: `OAUTH_STAFF_ONLY=true`, signed in as `devoauth-empty`, shows "Not available yet"
  - paused: `OAUTH_PAUSED=1` shows "Connecting apps is paused"
  - dark: `OAUTH_DARK=1` shows the app's ordinary 404 page
- **Reviewer sign-in:** the magic-link code field, taking the fixed 16-character reviewer code for `devoauth-reviewer@example.com`
- **Dark mode:** Profile → Appearance → Always dark, or `localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark"); location.reload()` in the console (`"auto"` to go back)

**What to decide.** These are the open copy and design questions. Nothing here changes the design. It only makes it reviewable.

1. **The "We haven't checked this app" warning.** Is the wording and its weight right for both variants: the web one ("only authorize it if you trust tools.example.com") and the device one ("only authorize it if you started it")?
2. **The warning colour in dark mode.** `.oauth-client__warning` uses `--color-highlight`, which is yellow in light mode and blue in dark. In dark mode the warning reads as information. Should it stay on `--color-highlight`, or move to a colour that warns in both themes?
3. **The access-picker descriptions.** "Read only" reads: "See your boards, cards, comments and the people in your account(s). It can't change anything." "Read and write" reads: "See everything you can, and act as you: create, edit, move, close and delete cards, comments and boards." Are the length and the list right?
4. **The disconnect dialog.** Is the title, "It loses its access to Fizzy right away…", the list of webhooks the app set up, and the unticked "Also remove these" right? It names another account only when a webhook is in one.
5. **The error copy** (new in this PR, see below). Each error now leads with a plain sentence. "For the app's developer: `<code>` · `<description>`" sits beneath it. Is the split right, and should the developer line be visible at all or tucked away? Should a dark server show "Not available yet" as bc3 does, rather than the plain 404 it shows now to keep the dark posture?
6. **Should Connected apps show before a first grant?** The profile entry only appears once something is connected, so someone who has never connected an app can't find the page. The page has an empty state for that case.

A smaller one: the personal access token form now says "Read and write", as consent and Connected apps do, but it still says "Read" where they say "Read only".

## What changed

- **`script/dev/oauth_states`**, ported from bc3's (bc3#12971). bc3's has no smoke test, so this one doesn't either. I ran it against a fresh development database: it seeds, runs again without creating duplicates, resets, and seeds again. Every URL it prints renders the state it names (status, heading, and the state's marker), and each posture and the reviewer code work with the server started as printed.
- **HTML error pages for the browser authorization flow.** `Oauth::BaseController#render_oauth_error` always rendered JSON. So an app not registered for the code grant, or a metadata document that couldn't be read, reached a person in a browser as a JSON body. A dark or paused server reached them as a bare 404 or 503, and so did switching without a browser session. Now `Oauth::AuthorizationsController` (and the switch, which inherits from it) renders the error page for HTML and keeps the OAuth JSON body for anything else:
  - a dark server renders the app's 404 page
  - a paused server renders a new "Connecting apps is paused" page
  - the token, registration and revocation endpoints keep their bare statuses whatever they're sent
- **Plain-language error copy.** The developer strings ("Invalid redirect_uri", "code_challenge is required"…) moved to the detail line under the plain sentence. `OauthHelper::OAUTH_ERROR_MESSAGES` gives each code a sentence, and a call site with more to say passes its own.
- **Copy consistency.**
  - The profile entry says "Connected apps", not "Connected Apps".
  - The token form and reveal say "Read and write", not "Read + Write".
  - The disconnect notice uses the "Unnamed app" fallback, as the list does.
- **Development toggles.** `OAUTH_PAUSED=1` and `OAUTH_STAFF_ONLY=true` join `OAUTH_DARK=1` in `config/environments/development.rb`.

**Files left alone.** Other open work edits `app/models/oauth/availability.rb`, `saas/app/models/identity/reviewer_sign_in.rb`, `app/controllers/oauth/tokens_controller.rb` and `app/models/oauth/client.rb`. This PR doesn't change any of them. The reviewer lines the script prints use the single-email variables, which work both before and after the per-partner change in #3257. `Oauth::BaseController`'s change is small: the dark and paused answers moved into `render_dark` and `render_paused`, which the authorization controller overrides.

**Tests.** `test/integration/oauth_error_pages_test.rb` covers:

- each error that used to reach a person as JSON or a bare status, now shown as a page
- the JSON answer still given when an app asks for it
- the content types: a browser `Accept`, `*/*`, `application/json`, `application/xml`
- the developer description shown beneath the plain sentence and never in its place
- bare statuses from the token and registration endpoints, even when they're sent `Accept: text/html`

The helper, the "Unnamed app" fallback in the notice, and the new labels have tests too. Existing tests that asserted JSON or the old wording from a browser request now assert the page, plus a JSON case where JSON is what they meant.

title: Bump rails-html-sanitizer to 1.7.2, loofah to 2.25.3, nokogiri to 1.19.5 (security)
body:
## Summary

Coordinated HTML-sanitizer security release.

- **rails-html-sanitizer** 1.7.1 → 1.7.2
- **loofah** 2.25.2 → 2.25.3
- **nokogiri** 1.19.4 → 1.19.5

Both `Gemfile.lock` and `Gemfile.saas.lock` move in lockstep (`bin/bundle-drift check` passes). nokogiri stays at 1.19.5; 1.19.6 fixes only a JRuby regression.

`RENDERING_VERSION` goes from `v2` to `v3`, retiring every cached fragment and page ETag. Expect a cold-cache load at rollout.

Release notes:
- https://github.com/rails/rails-html-sanitizer/releases/tag/v1.7.2
- https://github.com/flavorjones/loofah/releases/tag/v2.25.3
- https://github.com/sparklemotion/nokogiri/releases/tag/v1.19.5

## Why the three move together

rails-html-sanitizer 1.7.2 requires `loofah >= 2.25.3`, and loofah 2.25.3 requires `nokogiri >= 1.19.5`, whose HTML5 serializer escapes `<` and `>` in attribute values (loofah's [GHSA-h6v6-rg66-fqj4](https://github.com/flavorjones/loofah/security/advisories/GHSA-h6v6-rg66-fqj4)).

## Impact on fizzy

Fizzy sanitizes untrusted rich text (card description, comment body, board public description) through Action Text at render time. These fixes reach it:

- [GHSA-m3x9-938q-5767](https://github.com/flavorjones/loofah/security/advisories/GHSA-m3x9-938q-5767): `scrub_css` decoded CSS escapes and emitted a live `url()`. Reachable, because lexxy adds `style` to Action Text's allowed attributes.
- [GHSA-p9wj-w8xq-vjx6](https://github.com/flavorjones/loofah/security/advisories/GHSA-p9wj-w8xq-vjx6) and [GHSA-jcff-cj73-4w4f](https://github.com/flavorjones/loofah/security/advisories/GHSA-jcff-cj73-4w4f): `allowed_uri?` accepted `javascript:` and `data:text/html` URIs spelled with character references.
- [GHSA-h6v6-rg66-fqj4](https://github.com/flavorjones/loofah/security/advisories/GHSA-h6v6-rg66-fqj4): sanitized output could turn into new markup when a browser parsed it again.

Rich text sits in fragments keyed by record, so the gem bump alone would keep serving HTML sanitized under the old versions until it expires. The `RENDERING_VERSION` bump retires it, as #3233 did for crass.

Not reachable: the SVG `href` fixes (fizzy allows no SVG), the `noscript` escaping (not allowed), the rails-html-sanitizer scrubber race (Action Text passes the same allowlist on every call, and fizzy's own code never calls `sanitize`), and the quadratic-regexp fixes (Ruby 4.0.9).

No test or fixture output changes. Rich-text bodies with `<` or `>` in an attribute (such as an attachment's `content`) serialize as `<`/`>` on their next save; the parsed DOM is the same.

Full per-commit upgrade analysis for each gem is posted as comments below.

title: Bump rack and addressable past today's advisories
body:
## Why

The `Security` check's gem audit fails against `main`'s lockfiles since bundler-audit's advisory database flagged `rack` 3.2.7 and `addressable` 2.9.0. It blocks [#3261](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/pull/3261), the rails-html-sanitizer bump, which touches neither gem.

## What changes

`bin/bundle-both update --conservative --patch rack addressable`. Only these two entries and their checksums change, identically in `Gemfile.lock` and `Gemfile.saas.lock`. No other gem moves, and `bin/bundle-drift check` is in sync. addressable goes to 2.9.2 rather than 2.9.1 because 2.9.2 fixes regressions 2.9.1 introduced, such as a pure-Ruby `IDNA.to_unicode` up to 25 times slower.

| Gem | From → to | Advisories fixed |
|---|---|---|
| rack | 3.2.7 → 3.2.8 | Multipart parser memory exhaustion ([GHSA-5v64-555j-wjxm](https://github.com/rack/rack/security/advisories/GHSA-5v64-555j-wjxm), high). Invalid `Host` returned verbatim by `Rack::Request#host_with_port` and `#base_url` ([GHSA-2j8w-xcrc-x985](https://github.com/rack/rack/security/advisories/GHSA-2j8w-xcrc-x985), medium). `Rack::Static` `header_rules` bypass via dot segments ([GHSA-wvg4-6p58-3gh3](https://github.com/rack/rack/security/advisories/GHSA-wvg4-6p58-3gh3), medium). Multipart duplicate-`boundary` guard bypass ([GHSA-p8x9-v4hv-2w4g](https://github.com/rack/rack/security/advisories/GHSA-p8x9-v4hv-2w4g), low). |
| addressable | 2.9.0 → 2.9.2 | `URI.normalize_path` DoS and wrong `..` handling ([GHSA-qq38-m9mg-xjj5](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/security/advisories/GHSA-qq38-m9mg-xjj5), [GHSA-8gmh-2hhj-2hv9](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/security/advisories/GHSA-8gmh-2hhj-2hv9)). `Template#match`/`#extract` ReDoS ([GHSA-9f42-57jx-vpp3](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/security/advisories/GHSA-9f42-57jx-vpp3), [GHSA-j82w-28jv-3pmj](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/security/advisories/GHSA-j82w-28jv-3pmj), [GHSA-4w5q-wg7v-w6gp](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/security/advisories/GHSA-4w5q-wg7v-w6gp)). Misleading `display_uri` hosts from Punycode and bidi labels ([GHSA-9crm-g4mf-wc5j](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/security/advisories/GHSA-9crm-g4mf-wc5j), [GHSA-539f-xcgw-2gjg](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/security/advisories/GHSA-539f-xcgw-2gjg)). |

## Risk: low

- **Patch releases only.** Both are security and bug-fix releases within the same minor series, with no breaking API changes in either changelog ([rack](https://github.com/rack/rack/blob/v3.2.8/CHANGELOG.md), [addressable](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/blob/addressable-2.9.2/CHANGELOG.md)).
- **rack is on every request, but its fixes are narrow.** Multipart parsing, which Fizzy's uploads go through, now also rejects a second `boundary` parameter when the first is empty or quoted; browsers don't send those. Fizzy doesn't use `Rack::Static`. The `host_with_port` change doesn't reach Fizzy's requests: `ActionDispatch::Http::URL` overrides `host_with_port`, so `request.base_url`, which passkeys use as the WebAuthn origin, returns what it did on 3.2.7.
- **addressable runs at runtime through `geared_pagination`, and in SaaS through `signet`.** `geared_pagination` builds its `Link` header with `Addressable::URI.parse`, `#query_values=` and `#to_s`. `signet` comes in through `googleauth` for `action_push_native`. 2.9.2 fixes cached values going stale after a component setter; nothing it changes breaks those calls. `capybara`, `webmock` and `launchy` use it only in tests and development.
- **Rollback is a revert** of both lockfiles. There's no schema or data change.
- **Not exercised:** production traffic, a real browser upload, and Android push delivery through `googleauth`.

## Verification

- `bin/bundler-audit check --update`: no vulnerabilities, for both `Gemfile` and `Gemfile.saas`.
- `bin/rails test` (OSS, SQLite): 2581 runs, 0 failures, 0 errors. The SaaS suite runs in CI.

title: Pass CONSOLE_REASON through the query alias, and never send a blank CONSOLE_USER
body:
A console audit asks that sessions reading customer data carry the link that authorized them: the card, issue or Help Scout conversation. `rails query` can't prompt for a reason, so console1984 records every agent query as `rails query (via Claude Code)`. basecamp/console1984#169 appends `CONSOLE_REASON` to that reason. This passes it through the `query` alias:

```
CONSOLE_REASON=https://app.basecamp.com/…/cards/3 bin/kamal query "'Account.count'" -d production
```

It also fixes a second finding from the same audit: query sessions recorded under user `unknown`.

### CONSOLE_REASON through five parsers

On its way to `docker exec --env`, the value crosses five layers:

1. ERB, into a single-quoted YAML scalar
2. `Shellwords.split`, in `Kamal::Cli::Alias::Command`
3. Thor's `-e` hash, which splits each pair at its first colon, so a URL arrives whole
4. `String#dump`, in Kamal's `escape_shell_value`
5. the remote shell, which expands any `${…}`: Kamal escapes `$(` but leaves `${…}` in deliberately

Escaping for each layer in turn kept missing one. A Unicode line separator ends the YAML scalar and swallows the command. A C locale splits multibyte characters. `dump` adds a backslash before `#@` and `#{`. And `${…}` runs on the console host. So the header percent-encodes every byte outside a URL's own characters (`A-Za-z0-9`, space, `._~:/?#[]!&()*+,;=%-`). A link arrives unchanged, and anything else arrives as inert ASCII: `$` becomes `%24`, `é` becomes `%C3%A9`, a newline becomes `%0A`. When the variable is unset or blank, Kamal sends `--env CONSOLE_REASON` with no value, the same way it already handles an empty `CODEX_THREAD_ID`, and the container doesn't get the variable.

### CONSOLE_USER when USER is blank

In a sandbox, cron, launchd or `env -i`, `USER` can be unset. The aliases rendered a bare `CONSOLE_USER:`. In the unquoted `console`, `bash` and `ssh` aliases, that turns into `KEY: "…"`, a YAML mapping, and the whole file fails to parse (`mapping values are not allowed in this context`). Every kamal command fails, not just the console ones. The header now takes the first of `USER`, `LOGNAME` and the passwd name that is a plain login name (`\A[\w.@-]+\z`, matched on bytes), else `uid-<n>`. A name with a space, an apostrophe or invalid bytes is skipped, not interpolated.

So a blank `USER` can't be what recorded the `unknown` sessions through this alias. It breaks kamal before anything runs. Those sessions most likely came from a `bin/rails query` run without `-e CONSOLE_USER`, for example a hand-built `bin/kamal app exec` that doesn't go through the alias. console1984#169 proposes refusing a blank username, as an option rather than a default.

### Verified, without touching a host

A local harness renders this `deploy.yml` the way Kamal 2.12 does: ERB with `trim_mode: "-"`, then YAML. It expands `query` the way `Kamal::Cli::Alias::Command` does and runs Kamal's own Thor CLI, with `App#exec` stubbed. It then passes each `--env` argument Kamal would send through `sh -c`, standing in for the remote shell, and compares `CONSOLE_USER` and `CONSOLE_REASON` with literal expected values. **46 of 46 pass** for each of bc3, haystack and Fizzy: 23 cases, each in the default locale and under `LC_ALL=C`.

| Case | Arrives as |
|---|---|
| Basecamp card URL with `?`, `&`, `#__recording_…`; Help Scout URL | unchanged |
| `HS 12345: refund request`, `-p --hosts evil`, `:` | unchanged, as one value, not as options |
| `it's "quoted" \ back` | `it%27s %22quoted%22 %5C back` |
| `${X:=a[$(id)]}${!X} ${HOME} $HOME` and a backtick | every `$`, brace and backtick encoded; nothing expands |
| `#@ticket #{x} #$y` | `#%40ticket #%7Bx%7D #%24y`, with no backslash from `dump` |
| newline, tab, U+2028/U+2029, U+FFFF, non-ASCII, invalid UTF-8 | percent-encoded bytes |
| unset or empty | `--env CONSOLE_REASON` with no value, as today |
| `USER` unset, empty, whitespace, `a b`, `\xFF`, `é`; `LOGNAME="Jane O'Doe"` | the next plain login name |

To check that the harness can fail, I mutated the header three ways: removing `.b`, letting `$` through, and matching names on characters. Each mutation fails 1 to 4 cases.

### Landed dependencies

- basecamp/console1984#169, released as 0.2.5. This PR takes console1984 pinned to the GitHub tag `v0.2.5`, so `CONSOLE_REASON` is recorded.
- coworker#307: `bin/failed-jobs` renders the new alias.
- basecamp/audits1984#108: the audit UI shows a session's reason as text. This PR moves audits1984 to f99fc64.

### Fizzy doesn't record query sessions yet

`Gemfile.saas.lock` pins console1984 at 0.2.2 (`23419ec`). `Console1984::QueryAuditor` arrived in 0.2.3, so Fizzy's `rails query` sessions aren't recorded in `console1984_sessions` at all, whatever the reason or user. The bump this PR waits on brings in the auditor along with the reason. It also brings the other changes since 0.2.2: the Prism parser on Ruby 3.3+, and the `insert_all`/`upsert_all` fix to the auditable-tables shield.

title: Pin fizzy-mcp-server v0.2.2
body: Moves the `fizzy_mcp` accessory image from v0.2.1 to v0.2.2 (`sha256:8667578a…77a1e4`). v0.2.2 serves the authorization server's metadata (RFC 8414) at the MCP origin, at `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` and `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/mcp` (basecamp/fizzy-mcp-server#22), for clients of the older MCP authorization spec that look for it there. No configuration changes. App deploys do not reboot the accessory.

title: Register staging's MCP client, and add a dry run to the registry converge
body:
`Oauth::FirstPartyClients` should hold every OAuth client 37signals makes for Fizzy, each with a fixed `client_id`, so every environment converges to the same rows. A sweep of the clients we ship found one missing row, plus a way to check a converge before running it.

## Inventory

| Client | client_id | How it gets tokens |
|---|---|---|
| Personal access tokens (web UI, `fizzy-cli auth login` / `signup`, `fizzy-cli mcp`, `fizzy-mcp stdio`) | `fizzy-personal-access` | Already registered. The CLI and both local MCP servers take a personal access token (`FIZZY_TOKEN` or the CLI's keyring); `fizzy signup` mints one via `/my/access_tokens`. None of them runs an OAuth flow or sends a client_id. |
| Hosted MCP, production | `fizzy-mcp-server` | Already registered. |
| Hosted MCP, beta1 | `fizzy-mcp-server-beta1` | Already registered. It's the only beta with the exchange turned on. |
| **Hosted MCP, staging** | **`fizzy-mcp-server-staging`** (new) | The server runs on staging but is dark: no `FIZZY_OAUTH_MCP_RESOURCES` and no exchange client set. Once staging is lit, its row would have come from `oauth:provision_mcp_client`, outside the registry. |
| iOS and Android apps | none | They sign in with a magic link and a cookie session, not OAuth. |
| fizzy-sdk | none | Its AGENTS.md says "two auth strategies, and no OAuth". |
| Third-party MCP clients (Claude, ChatGPT, …) | generated / CIMD URL | Dynamic registration or Client ID Metadata Documents. These are self-registered and don't belong in the registry. |

Fizzy has no device-authorization grant, so no CLI client is waiting on one.

## Changes

- `HOSTED_MCP_SERVERS` gains staging's resource → `fizzy-mcp-server-staging`. Like the other hosted clients, it converges only where `FIZZY_OAUTH_MCP_RESOURCES` names its resource, so until staging is lit it is written nowhere. Staging has its own database and could reuse `fizzy-mcp-server`. A separate id keeps the map one-to-one, which is what `provision_mcp_server!` relies on to pair a resource with its client in both directions. There's a test that holds that invariant.
- `DRY_RUN=1 bin/rails oauth:provision_first_party_clients` prints, for each client, `would be created` / `would converge` / `unchanged`, then each attribute as `from -> to`. Secret digests show only as `[digest]`. It also prints validation errors and any client still awaiting a secret, and writes nothing. It runs through the new `Oauth::FirstPartyClients.plan`, which shares one method (`converging`) with `converge!`, so the dry run assigns exactly what a converge would save and raises wherever a converge would refuse to repoint a client.

## Open

- Choosing `fizzy-mcp-server-staging` over reusing `fizzy-mcp-server` is a call to make in review. When staging's exchange is turned on, its deploy file needs `FIZZY_MCP_EXCHANGE_CLIENT_ID` to match. That env isn't added here, because staging is still dark; `deploy.staging.yml` only gains a comment naming the client.

## Tests

`bin/rails test test/models/oauth test/integration/oauth_token_exchange_test.rb test/controllers/my/access_tokens_controller_test.rb`: 269 tests, 0 failures. `test/models/oauth/first_party_clients_test.rb` together with `test/tasks/oauth_provision_first_party_clients_task_test.rb`: 25 tests, 0 failures. Changing `plan` to call `converge!` makes the new dry-run tests fail, as they should. The task test clears any `DRY_RUN` in the shell during setup and puts it back in teardown. Without that, an exported `DRY_RUN=1` made the existing converge test run as a dry run and fail.

title: Upgrade Rails to 8b06b0eb, with today's security fixes
body:
## Motivation Fizzy's Rails pin, `4658033f`, predates today's [Rails security release](https://rubyonrails.org/2026/11/4/Rails-8.0.5.2-and-8.1.4.1-have-been-released). This moves it to rails/rails main at [`8b06b0eb`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/8b06b0eb98315cbbd6d7f526112cd8d909ff787c), which contains every fix in that release through the merge [`6782df4a`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/6782df4a5e14aeea04a5a66cb4f3628b34f88f86). Fizzy runs edge Rails, so this bump is how it gets them. ## Details Both `Gemfile.lock` and `Gemfile.saas.lock` move only the Rails `revision:` line; no other gem moves, and `bin/bundle-drift` is clean. Three upstream changes need app changes: 1. [rails/rails@ccb4c626](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/ccb4c626f9ae55883362acb8572fe91ce8eb1490) removed `Variant#process_from_io`, which the SaaS override in `saas/lib/fizzy/saas/unprocessable_attachments.rb` called. Every form upload with an immediate variant (avatars, Action Text embeds) raised `NoMethodError`. The override now calls `processed` and rewinds once after the loop, as upstream does. `processed` reads the uploaded file through `Blob#open`, which reuses the local io, so nothing is downloaded. The existing SaaS tests caught this. 2. [rails/rails@c3ffcf4d](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/c3ffcf4d) deprecated `ColumnDefinition#limit`, which the SQLite CHECK-constraint shim in `config/initializers/table_definition_column_limits.rb` read, printing a warning for every string and text column on each schema load. It now reads `options[:limit]`. 3. [rails/rails@475118e1](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/475118e11393c2675cc84cfb580575afb841bbde) ([GHSA-2gff-2mmg-m73p](https://github.com/rails/rails/security/advisories/GHSA-2gff-2mmg-m73p)) makes `RemoteIp` raise `IpSpoofAttackError` when `Forwarded` and `X-Forwarded-For` name different clients. Today a client can send `Forwarded` to choose its own `remote_ip`, because `RemoteIp` prefers it over the `X-Forwarded-For` that `TrackTrueClientIp` sets; after the bump that request would 500 instead. `TrackTrueClientIp` now deletes `Forwarded` whenever True-Client-IP is present, consistent with its job of collapsing the chain to the one address we trust. Requests without True-Client-IP keep upstream behavior; on that path the client already controls `X-Forwarded-For`. I made this call rather than leave the 500s; it is easy to revert if someone prefers otherwise. ## Additional information Checks for whoever deploys, from the plan: - On staging, confirm no hop (Cloudflare, the F5, kamal-proxy) adds a `Forwarded` header. Rack prefers `Forwarded`'s `proto=` and `host=` for the request scheme and host, so a hop relying on it without also setting `X-Forwarded-Proto` would break once the header is dropped. - On staging, register and sign in with a passkey, and confirm the first GET of the login page sets no session cookie ([rails/rails@c82ad5f7](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/c82ad5f7): no authenticity tokens render under fizzy's `:header_only` CSRF strategy). - On staging, `curl -I` a `public: true` endpoint for the new `Vary: Accept, X-Requested-With` header, then watch the CDN hit rate after deploy ([rails/rails@e38dd281](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/e38dd281d340d28bda39877ee83665f092091de2)). - Carried over from #3251's plan: EXPLAIN the filtered card count on MySQL (`d6a7aac0`), spot-check JSON collection endpoints, smoke-test static files. The Trilogy-era mitigations listed on the [mitigations card](https://app.basecamp.com/2914079/buckets/1666/card_tables/cards/10434852267) stay. Fizzy moved to `mysql2` in #3240, and nothing in this range makes the remaining adapter-independent ones (SQL redaction, client-side DB timeouts, `mysql_ssl_mode.rb`) unnecessary. [GHSA-3f4q-8x5m-76v8](https://github.com/rails/rails/security/advisories/GHSA-3f4q-8x5m-76v8) ([rails/rails@29468ede](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/29468ede23869cdafa2cc98cdb81dfafb9ba7cf0), an ffmpeg format allowlist) does not reach SaaS video processing, because the Hotcell server builds its own ffmpeg command line. That needs raising with the Hotcell owners; it is outside this PR. This overlaps #3251 by @djmb, which moves the pin to `83ddc9f6`; this PR covers that range too and goes further, to include the security release. Full plan: [`upgrade-analysis/fizzy-20261104-rails_4658033f..8b06b0eb.md`](https://github.com/basecamp/37signals-hq/blob/34f69ecd90c709bbcfc63531905e912b3e3d82fe/upgrade-analysis/fizzy-20261104-rails_4658033f..8b06b0eb.md), also posted below as a comment.
Security-release commits in 8b06b0eb - [`c0c32eae`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/c0c32eaec891fcdea5cb5acba738a41efd944245) Ship an ImageMagick security policy for every MiniMagick process - [`ccb4c626`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/ccb4c626f9ae55883362acb8572fe91ce8eb1490) Active Storage: tempfile extension must match the blob's content type - [`baa47af0`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/baa47af0e9024e24a0fbae48106b733f4c93c4f1) Return self from `Parameters#each_key` with a block - [`475118e1`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/475118e11393c2675cc84cfb580575afb841bbde) Detect conflicts in Forwarded and X-Forwarded-For in ActionDispatch::RemoteIp - [`0f8a40f8`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/0f8a40f88326029367a4c4b5654e62bcd5583b60) Avoid dynamic regexp in safe_constantize LoadError handling - [`943ee1ed`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/943ee1ed7e1ac8c604ce0e55a5a7596a89ffbda3) Require rails-html-sanitizer 1.7.2 or later - [`187fae2e`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/187fae2e9c6b14e982e1ec96087f6ffe54c89e87) Escape the phrase substituted into highlight's :highlighter - [`ce885768`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/ce8857688531f3e2001ffcdf58d147adeb168728) Fix `strip_tags` to encode `"` and `'` in its output - [`99a3247e`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/99a3247ebc02de86c5fdc9a5fd7c1ce0143c5d14) Skip tag attribute names that are blank once converted to a string - [`53b1361d`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/53b1361d8a09479e7fa7ac4a4f3cb85d2a490722) ActiveSupport::MessagePack preserve SafeBuffer html_safe status - [`87c6264b`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/87c6264b2b9b72cf3d9a76cc0cefb1f844250ebe) Avoid blocking Live buffer termination - [`c447c105`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/c447c10552c774fbc5ccb61fb97e4561fd7ce2ac) Preserve committed Active Storage streams after errors - [`0e6a6afe`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/0e6a6afe3cb7f4868fddba72a929a1e7df1a8d3d) Sanitize Active Storage filename parts - [`c14e3309`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/c14e3309903ac9d2d494cd2eedc821ccc2551f55) Sign GCS direct uploads with V2 when cache_control is set - [`d5615b8e`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/d5615b8eb442cd6104dc932c7bf83cb0b046c883) Enforce the content length on GCS direct uploads - [`8e4d875b`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/8e4d875b2e1190adca3d565f451ee7747bf57873) Skip writing a CacheStore session deleted mid-request - [`1640b94e`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/1640b94e4cdbd783104b89bd25afae571919ce86) Don't write upgraded cookies to a response that skips the session - [`e38dd281`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/e38dd281d340d28bda39877ee83665f092091de2) Vary rendered responses by negotiation headers - [`29468ede`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/29468ede23869cdafa2cc98cdb81dfafb9ba7cf0) Restrict the formats ffmpeg and ffprobe may open - [`a8422c5f`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/a8422c5f3919d9dcccba75fb998cdebec922bf39) Reject Mailgun timestamps from the future - [`7723e497`](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/7723e497178aa8348632807566bf408fc078958e) Apply `cookies_same_site_protection` to every session store

title: Serve uploaded files as binary unless we recognize their type
body:
Hardens how uploaded files are served. A blob's content type is the uploader's declaration whenever the bytes can't be identified, and an import carries whatever type its archive names. Rails picks the served type from a deny-list, which we've been extending, and a deny-list only names the types someone thought of.

### What changes

**Serve as binary unless we recognize the type.** `lib/rails_ext/active_storage_serve_unknown_types_as_binary.rb` replaces the deny-list regex in `active_storage_authorization.rb`. It overrides `forcibly_serve_as_binary?`, the one decision Rails reads for the served type, the forced attachment disposition and the type stored with the service on upload, so the signed storage URL, the disk route and the upload all follow it. Kept as-is:

| Type | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `ActiveStorage.content_types_allowed_inline` (images, PDF) | Displayed inline today. Nothing in this list changes disposition. |
| `audio/*`, `video/*` | `<audio>` and `<video>` in `active_storage/blobs/web/_representation` point at the file |
| `image/heic`, `image/heif` | Rails' `variable_content_types` includes them, so we convert them, while a card background (`cards/display/common/_background`) and the editor point at the original |
| `application/zip` | `ZipFile` writes account and user exports with it |

Everything else goes out as `application/octet-stream` with an attachment disposition. Parameters and case are ignored when matching and kept when serving. A blank type, a comma anywhere (browsers read a comma list as several types), control characters and non-ASCII are always binary.

Files outside that list were already downloads, so only their declared type changes; they keep their filename through `Content-Disposition`.

**Close the Active Storage proxy routes.** They now answer 404 before looking up the blob, as HEY's do.

- Nothing generates these URLs. `rg` for `rails_storage_proxy`, `rails_service_blob_proxy`, `representation_proxy` and `resolve_model_to_route` finds only tests in this repo, so `rails_blob_path` and `url_for` use Rails' default, the redirect route. fizzy-cli, fizzy-mcp-server, fizzy-sdk, fizzy-ios, fizzy-android, fizzy-site and fizzy-popper have no references either.
- Production has next to no traffic on them over the past week, and none on the representation proxy, against steady traffic on the redirect routes.
- The redirect leaves the app's origin on S3-backed deployments. On the disk service `/rails/active_storage/disk` still answers from the app's origin, so the type list above is what covers self-hosted installs.
- `ActiveStorage::Authorize` stays on these controllers, so removing the 404 later can't open them to everyone.

### Tests

`test/integration/active_storage_served_content_types_test.rb` serves blobs through the redirect route and follows it to the bytes.

- Unrecognized types: scripts, HTML and Turbo Stream variants, JSON, CSS, SVG, XML, blank and nil are binary with `nosniff` and attachment, including when asked for `disposition=inline`.
- Spelling: parameters, case, comma lists, control characters and non-ASCII.
- The regression guard for what must keep working: images and PDFs stay inline, audio, video, HEIC and HEIF keep their type, documents download under their own filename, both export kinds stay `application/zip` attachments, an avatar displays for an anonymous visitor, and a published card's background, embedded image, `<video>` and `<audio>` each display for an anonymous visitor, following the URLs the public page actually renders.

Without the first commit's new file, 13 of the 46 tests in the three affected files fail. Without the 404, 4 fail.

`pagination_blob_html_xss_test.rb` and `active_storage_authorization_test.rb` read through the proxy route, so they now use the redirect route, or assert the 404. The tests of the proxy's `Cache-Control` and its 422 went with the route.

### Not changed

- Blob authorization, and anything that displays inline today.
- No new third party and no new personal data.

title: Keep pagination links on the page's own route
body:
A pagination link passes the current request to `url_for` as options, minus a list of the keys `url_for` treats as controls. That list has grown one key at a time, and anything not on it still steers the link: a query could name a different route, or add a format to the path, and the page would render a next-page link pointing there.

Query params shouldn't be able to choose a pagination link's route, so now they can't reach route generation at all. The query goes through `url_for(params:)`, where every key can only come back out as a query parameter. The route comes from the request's own path parameters, which `url_for` recalls.

- `URL_FOR_CONTROL_OPTIONS`, `forwardable_request_params` and its `permit!` go away, and so does the Brakeman ignore for it.
- Filters, search terms and any other query params carry over as before. `page` is replaced.
- Form params no longer carry over. A Turbo Stream response to a POST used to copy the form's body, authenticity token included, into its next-page link.
- A control key in the query now comes back as a plain, inert query param rather than being dropped.

`test/integration/pagination_links_test.rb` and `test/controllers/searches_controller_test.rb` together render each of the 12 views that paginate, through real routing, with and without such a query, and one test follows a link. `test/helpers/pagination_helper_test.rb` now checks the options `url_for` recognizes, one at a time.

The other places that build links from a request were checked and don't need changing: they pass named keys or a fixed permit list (`Filter#as_params`, the OAuth switch's `AUTHORIZATION_PARAMS`, `join_path`, the unsubscribe path).

title: Cap a join code's usage limit above the max on import and reset
body:
Join codes saved before the usage limit cap landed in fa118a7d8 (2025-12-10) can hold a `usage_limit` above `Account::JoinCode::USAGE_LIMIT_MAX`. Between widening the column to bigint on 2025-11-17 and that commit, the edit form had no upper bound. Validation only runs on save, so those rows sat there quietly until something saved them:

- The account import copied the limit with `update!` ([account_record_set.rb:35](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/9a30a77274b185afcd2bf192a4c5a3e5d63a8cfd/app/models/account/data_transfer/account_record_set.rb#L35)). A genuine export of such an account failed in `Account::DataImportJob` with `RecordInvalid: Usage limit cannot be larger than the population of the planet`. `RecordInvalid` isn't a terminal error, so the import ended with no failure reason, and a retry hit the same row again.
- `JoinCode#reset` calls `save!`, so Reset on a live account with one of these rows raised the same error.

Both now go through `JoinCode#cap_usage_limit`, which lowers the limit to the max before saving. Stanko picked capping over dropping the counters on the On Call card. Editing the limit by hand is unchanged: an over-cap value typed into the form or sent to the API is still rejected.

Tests: one round-trip import test with an over-cap limit and one reset test. Both failed on main with that `RecordInvalid` and pass with the change. `bin/ci` passed locally in OSS/SQLite mode, signoff included.

title: Reject an import whose join code limits aren't integers
body:
Two account imports failed on a hand-built zip whose `data/account.json` carried `"usage_limit": null` in `join_code`. Fizzy can't export a null limit (the column is `NOT NULL DEFAULT 10`), but the check step accepted it and the file only blew up in `process`: before #3269 as `RecordInvalid` with the custom "cannot be larger than the population of the planet" message, which also covers the not-a-number case and so hid the cause; after #3269 as `NoMethodError` in `cap_usage_limit`.

## Fix

`AccountRecordSet#check_record` now requires `usage_count` and `usage_limit` to be integers, next to the existing `join_code` shape checks. `Account::Import#check` already maps `IntegrityError` to `failure_reason: invalid_export`, and the job runs `check` before `process`, so the file is rejected before anything is written.

## Test

A new `Account::ImportTest` case builds a zip with only `data/account.json` and `usage_limit: nil` and asserts that `check` raises `IntegrityError` and the import fails with `invalid_export`. It fails on `main` ("IntegrityError expected but nothing was raised") and passes with the fix.

Possible follow-up, not done here: the custom `message:` on `validates :usage_limit, numericality:` in `Account::JoinCode` also covers the not-a-number error, so splitting it would make that validation failure legible if it ever recurs.

title: Rename the OAuth staff gate to CONNECTED_APPS_PREVIEW, and admit listed reviewers
body:
Renames the OAuth staff gate to say what it gates, and lets reviewers through it, so connected apps can be reviewed ahead of launch without making anyone staff.

## What the gate covered before

`OAUTH_STAFF_ONLY=true` (`config.x.oauth.staff_only`) limits OAuth to 37signals staff, whichever client asks: DCR clients, Client ID Metadata Document clients, pilot clients and the hosted MCP server's delegation. The SaaS engine already admits the directory reviewers it signs in (`Identity::ReviewerSignIn`) through an extension hook. Every site goes through one predicate, `Oauth::Availability.admits?`:

- consent, `Oauth::AuthorizationsController#require_admitted_identity`, which renders the refusal page or answers JSON `access_denied`
- code redemption and refresh, `Oauth::TokensController#require_admitted_identity` and `#require_admitted_grant_owner`
- token use, `Identity::AccessToken#honored_identity?`, and through it token exchange, since a subject token must be `honored?`
- push delivery, `Push::Subscription.deliverable_to`

Personal access tokens, discovery, revocation and Connected Apps management aren't gated. Fizzy has no device flow. Production, staging and every beta set it to `"true"`. OAuth itself is lit only on production and beta1.

## What changes

- **Name.** `CONNECTED_APPS_PREVIEW` replaces `OAUTH_STAFF_ONLY` in every deploy file. The code names follow it: `connected_apps_preview?`, `previewer?`, `admit_as_reviewer`, and the `preview` refusal view.
- **Who previews.** `admits?(identity)` is `!connected_apps_preview? || previewer?(identity)`, and `previewer?` is `staff? || reviewer?`. A reviewer is either an identity id listed in `CONNECTED_APPS_PREVIEW_REVIEWERS` or someone an extension admits (the directory reviewers, unchanged). Reviewers get exactly what staff get at every site above. They aren't staff, so `/admin` stays closed to them.
- **Reviewer list.** A deploy secret listing identity ids, separated by commas or spaces. It's parsed once at boot. Whitespace and case are tolerated, and an entry that isn't an identity id is skipped. The skip is logged as a warning and reported as an `oauth.preview.reviewers_skipped` audit event, which the structured log keeps at any log level. Both give the count, never the entry. Unset or empty means no reviewers. It's referenced in `env.secret` and `.kamal/secrets.*` for production and the betas. Staging is dark, so it isn't added there yet.
- **Old name for one release.** `OAUTH_STAFF_ONLY` still counts while `CONNECTED_APPS_PREVIEW` is unset or blank, so a destination deployed with a stale config stays in preview instead of opening. The deploy files also keep `OAUTH_STAFF_ONLY: "true"` next to the new name, because a Kamal rollback boots an older image with the current config, and an image from before the rename reads only the old name. If both are set, the new name wins. If neither is set, the preview is off, the same default as today, which is what OSS installs rely on. There's a TODO to drop the old name.
- **Copy.** Refused people now read "Connecting apps to Fizzy is in preview…", on the page and in the OAuth error descriptions.

No migrations.

## Before deploying

The production and beta deploy secrets must hold a `CONNECTED_APPS_PREVIEW_REVIEWERS` entry before the first deploy of this branch. Otherwise `kamal secrets fetch` can't read it and the deploy stops. The entry needs a value for `kamal secrets extract` to return. A lone `,` parses to no reviewers.

## Tests

- Unit tests in `Oauth::AvailabilityTest` cover: staff are admitted; a listed reviewer id is admitted; an identity outside the list is refused; an empty, nil or junk list admits no reviewers (the junk warning is checked too); the old env name is honored and the new name takes precedence; with the preview off, everyone is admitted.
- Integration tests: a listed reviewer consents, redeems, uses, refreshes and exchanges, and keeps push delivery. Once delisted, they're refused at consent, redemption, refresh and token use. The existing tests that refuse everyone else at every site are kept.
- Mutation check: dropping `reviewer?`, dropping the id list, dropping the staff check, dropping the old-name fallback, dropping `.presence`, accepting junk, dropping the downcase, and ignoring the switch each fail at least one test (8 of 8).

title: Record unreachable networks as a failed webhook delivery
body:
A `Webhook::DeliveryJob` failed in production on 2026-11-06 with:

```
Errno::ENETUNREACH: Failed to open TCP connection to 2606:4700:4700::1111:80 (Network is unreachable)
```

The webhook's host only had a public IPv6 address, and our job containers don't have an IPv6 route. `Webhook::Delivery#perform_request` already turns unreachable hosts into `destination_unreachable`, but its rescue list skipped this errno. So the error reached `deliver`'s bare `rescue`, the delivery was marked errored, the job failed, and the delinquency tracker never counted the attempt.

This PR adds 3 errnos to the `destination_unreachable` rescue. Each one means we can't reach an IPv6-only host:

- `ENETUNREACH`: no route to the network (the production failure)
- `EADDRNOTAVAIL`: a route exists, but there isn't a usable source address
- `EAFNOSUPPORT`: the host doesn't support IPv6 at all

We don't need to prefer IPv4 when picking the address. [Surfguard already returns IPv4 before IPv6](https://github.com/basecamp/surfguard/blob/71cac69a592d9ef63ce27600eb26bdf94803a3eb/lib/surfguard.rb#L99-L106), so dual-stack targets connect over IPv4 today.

title: Fail an import cleanly when its data doesn't fit a column
body:
On Call: https://app.basecamp.com/2914079/buckets/27/card_tables/cards/10483307634

Someone uploaded 24 hand-built archives from 1 IP with curl this morning. One had a user id too long for `binary(16)`, and the import died with `ActiveRecord::ValueTooLong`. Only `IntegrityError` counts as terminal for `Account::DataImportJob`, so the error retried, landed in failed jobs and paged on call. Duplicate keys (#3068) and join code limits failed the same way before this.

## Changes

- `RecordSet#import` turns the errors bad data causes into `IntegrityError`: `ValueTooLong`, `RangeError` (both Active Record's and Active Model's), `NotNullViolation`, `CheckViolation` (SQLite's version of "too long"), `RecordInvalid` and `SerializationTypeMismatch`.
- `RecordSet#load` treats a record that isn't JSON, or isn't a JSON object, as invalid. Sentry caught a `JSON::ParserError` from this job on Oct 20.
- `discard_on(*TERMINAL_ERRORS, report: true)`: each discarded import sends 1 Sentry event, without a retry or a failed job.

## What this doesn't cover

I kept the list of errors named on purpose and didn't rescue `StatementInvalid`. During a failover, MySQL's read-only error comes back as a plain `StatementInvalid`, and those imports should retry. So a crafted value MySQL rejects without a more specific error, like `Incorrect datetime value`, still retries and pages. The comment above the list says so.

## Testing

- A reviewer threw 21 crafted archives at the import on both databases. With this PR, every one that used to retry now fails cleanly, except bad dates on MySQL (above) and a unique key sent as a JSON hash.
- 5 of the new tests run real crafted data on both adapters. The deadlock test guards that transient errors still retry.
- `test/models/account` and `test/jobs/account` pass on SQLite and MySQL (108 tests).

title: Serve the activities feed from one cache read per page
body:
The activities feed now serves a 100-row page in about half the time, with 28 queries instead of 91. Each activity is cached whole, and a page reads all of its activities from the cache at once. Before, every activity read its card or comment, board and creator from the cache one query at a time, and rebuilt its description and URLs on every request.

On-call card: [[Fizzy] Activities API is slow and costly to poll](https://app.basecamp.com/2914079/buckets/27/card_tables/cards/10483559130).

## API change

`description` no longer changes with who reads it. An assignee used to see "David will handle …", and someone unassigned saw "… unassigned yourself". Now everyone gets the third-person sentence that webhook deliveries already send: "David assigned JZ to …". A cached activity can't depend on the reader. The HTML timeline keeps its wording.

## Numbers

Dev copy with 2M events, 200k boards and production view settings. One user sees 1,205 events on 45 boards. Median of 30 warm requests:

| Page | Rows | Before | After | Queries |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 15 | 26.9ms | 19.0ms | 36 → 22 |
| 4 | 100 | 92.2ms | 46.6ms | 91 → 28 |
| 9 | 100 | 89.3ms | 46.4ms | 91 → 28 |

I measured these with an earlier, larger cache key, so a hit now costs the same or less. Production's cache reads cross the network, so the saving there should be bigger.

The SQL isn't the cost: the main query takes about 2ms at any offset.

<details>
<summary>EXPLAIN ANALYZE, page 12</summary>

```
-> Limit/Offset: 100/1105 row(s)  (actual time=1.83..1.84 rows=100 loops=1)
    -> Sort: events.created_at DESC, events.id DESC, limit input to 1205 row(s) per chunk  (actual time=1.74..1.82 rows=1205 loops=1)
        -> Nested loop inner join  (actual time=0.0161..1.23 rows=1205 loops=1)
            -> Nested loop inner join  (actual time=0.0112..0.078 rows=45 loops=1)
                -> Index lookup on accesses using index_accesses_on_user_id (user_id=...)  (rows=45 loops=1)
                -> Single-row covering index lookup on boards using PRIMARY (id=accesses.board_id)  (rows=1 loops=45)
            -> Filter: (events.action in (...12 actions...))  (rows=26.8 loops=45)
                -> Index lookup on events using index_events_on_board_id (board_id=accesses.board_id)  (rows=26.8 loops=45)
```

</details>

## Cache key

The key is the event and its card: `cached: ->(event) { [ event, event.card ] }`.

- **Cards and comments.** Any change to a card updates the card, and a comment edit touches its card, so both show up on the next request.
- **Boards.** A board rename touches all its cards, so it shows up right away. The board itself isn't in the key: every card change touches its board, so a board key would expire every activity on a busy board all the time. Other board changes, like publishing, show up the next time the activity's card changes. Cached cards already work that way.
- **Users.** A renamed creator or assignee shows up the next time the card changes. The rest of the app doesn't expire caches on user renames either, and the API docs say these fields "may reflect current resource state".

## Jbuilder patch

Jbuilder doesn't register its dependency tracker, so editing a nested partial like `cards/_card.json.jbuilder` wouldn't expire the cached activities that embed it. `lib/rails_ext/jbuilder_dependency_tracker.rb` registers the tracker. bc3 has the same patch until [rails/jbuilder#620](https://github.com/rails/jbuilder/pull/620) ships. Every cached JSON fragment misses once after deploy.

## Not in this PR

- A `since` or cursor param for pollers. [#2873](https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/pull/2873) only filters by day.
- `fresh_when`. This poller doesn't send `If-None-Match`, so it wouldn't help.
- The HTML day timeline has stale card titles and shares assignment wording between viewers. That needs its own PR, because of the timeline's page cache.

## After deploy

- Compare df-iad p99 with and without `ActivitiesController`.
- Track the activity cache hit rate for a day before closing the card.

No new third parties or personal data.
