title: Bump rack to 3.2.9 for the November 20 rack advisories
body:
Moves rack from 3.2.8 to 3.2.9 in both `Gemfile.lock` and `Gemfile.saas.lock`. Nothing else changes; `bin/bundle-drift check` says the two are in sync.

I edited the two rack lines and their checksums by hand rather than with `bundle lock --update rack --conservative`: local Bundler 4.0.20 also rewrote `BUNDLED WITH` and dropped the generic-platform nokogiri, sqlite3 and mini_portile2 entries. The checksum is rubygems.org's for rack-3.2.9, and a frozen `bundle install` passes for both Gemfiles.

| Advisory | Severity | What |
|---|---|---|
| [GHSA-58mf-c3jj-277p](https://github.com/rack/rack/security/advisories/GHSA-58mf-c3jj-277p) | high | Multipart parser searches the load path for every unknown part `charset`: CPU exhaustion |
| [GHSA-f7cc-57h7-qrcg](https://github.com/rack/rack/security/advisories/GHSA-f7cc-57h7-qrcg) | medium | `Rack::QueryParser` memory amplification on runs of spaces or brackets |
| [GHSA-frgv-948x-h96g](https://github.com/rack/rack/security/advisories/GHSA-frgv-948x-h96g) | medium | Multipart part headers keep CRLF in parameter names |
| [GHSA-r243-pfwh-7rpx](https://github.com/rack/rack/security/advisories/GHSA-r243-pfwh-7rpx) | low | Multipart boundary taken by substring match |
| [GHSA-mhj6-xc86-54m8](https://github.com/rack/rack/security/advisories/GHSA-mhj6-xc86-54m8) | medium | `Rack::Directory` lists outside its root through a symlink |

rack published these on its own repo on 2026-11-20. None is in GitHub's advisory database yet, so Dependabot won't open this.

**GHSA-mhj6 doesn't reach Fizzy.** Nothing in the app, its config or its loaded gems (OSS or SaaS bundle) mounts `Rack::Directory` (`rg 'Rack::Directory'` over the repo and every gem in `bundle list --paths` for both Gemfiles finds only a web-console test template). The bump fixes it anyway.

**Tests:** CI (SaaS) is green on 86a218c: Test (OSS) and Test (SaaS), each on MySQL and SQLite, plus Lint, Security, Gemfile drift and CodeQL. The first SaaS MySQL run timed out installing apt packages; the rerun passed.

**Verify where it runs**, after deploy. Production loads `Gemfile.saas.lock` (`BUNDLE_GEMFILE=Gemfile.saas` in the image):

```
bin/kamal app exec -d production --reuse 'bundle exec ruby -e "puts Gem.loaded_specs[%q(rack)].full_name"'
```

It should print rack-3.2.9. Use `-d staging`, `-d beta` or `-d beta1` for the others.

title: Let Perplexity connect to the Fizzy MCP by its metadata document
body:
Perplexity's MCP connector identifies by its Client ID Metadata Document, `https://www.perplexity.ai/.well-known/mcp-client.json`. `www.perplexity.ai` isn't a recognized CIMD host, so the authorization endpoint treats it as an unknown client.

- Adds `www.perplexity.ai` to `OAUTH_CIMD_ALLOWED_HOSTS` in `saas/config/deploy.yml`, and to the development and test lists. Exact host match as before: `perplexity.ai`, `evil.www.perplexity.ai` and `www.perplexity.ai.example.com` stay unrecognized (`url_test.rb`).
- The fixture is Perplexity's published document as of 2026-11-24. It names no `scope`, so it's provisioned with read and write, and its `none` auth method, `authorization_code` grant and 8 https callbacks pass `Oauth::ClientMetadata::Document`. The new integration test carries it through consent and token exchange on its `www.perplexity.ai` callback.
- `saas/test/lib/oauth_cimd_allowed_hosts_test.rb` reads the production deploy configuration through Kamal and holds its host list equal to the test environment's, so a host the tests connect through is one production recognizes.
- Corrects the `deploy.yml` comment that said no destination enables metadata documents.

Personal data: no new service on our side. Perplexity receives a token only when someone connects it and approves consent, as with Claude and ChatGPT.

title: Port the open tier of Client ID Metadata Documents from bc3, dark
body:
Ports bc3's open tier of Client ID Metadata Documents to Fizzy, **dark**. Today Fizzy fetches a metadata document only from an allowlisted host (`OAUTH_CIMD_ALLOWED_HOSTS`). With the open tier on, any https host that publishes a valid document may request consent, with a warning that we don't know the app.

**No migration.** An earlier revision added bc3's `oauth_cimd_domain_quotas` table. It's gone: `git diff main...HEAD -- db/` is empty, `schema.rb` and `schema_sqlite.rb` included. The table was never created on beta1 or staging.

## How the open tier is contained

Anyone can publish a document, so what matters is how many client rows, and how many fetches, an open tier lets someone cause. Instead of bc3's per-registrable-domain row quota (25 clients per domain per 30 days), this uses five controls:

1. **The sweep.** An open-tier client with no grant, and untouched for a day, is removed by the hourly `Oauth::Client.cleanup` (new step `idle_open_tier_clients`, rechecked under the row lock like the existing one). It comes back from its document the next time someone authorizes it. Rows now last only while someone holds a grant. Allowlisted hosts' clients keep `UNUSED_RETENTION`.
   - Fizzy writes an open-tier row only on the authorization POST. That same POST touches it at consent, so "untouched since written" (the DCR rule) would spare nearly every row, including those consented to and never redeemed. The rule here is "no grant and untouched for a day". A code lives a minute, so a row untouched for a day has no code out.
   - A row disconnected from its last grant also goes after a day rather than 30. It self-heals.
   - A sweep that lands between the lookup and the consent touch gives the existing "Fizzy doesn't recognize this app… start again" page, as for DCR. Starting again provisions the row afresh.
2. **A block list** (`OAUTH_CIMD_BLOCKED_DOMAINS`, space-separated, case-insensitive). An entry blocks its own host and every host under it at a label boundary: `example.com` blocks all of it, and `tools.example.com` only that part. Hosts compare as DNS names, case-folded and with a trailing dot ignored, so `tools.example.com.` doesn't slip past.
   - It applies to either tier, before any fetch, and to clients already provisioned. It answers as an unknown client, so the block isn't advertised.
   - Grants already issued keep working, since the token endpoint never resolves documents. Revoking those is a separate operator step.
   - Fizzy clients have no per-client disable, so this is the incident tool short of turning the whole open tier off.
3. **A site-wide domain fetch budget.** The open tier's 60-an-hour budget per registrable domain is now shared by everyone (`oauth:client_metadata:domain:<domain>`), as bc3's is. Per person, each new account would add another domain's worth of new clients an hour.
   - The per-URL budget and the allowlisted per-host budget stay per person, for the reason in the resolver's header: a shared budget there would let one person's reloads refuse an allowlisted app's first authorization to everyone.
   - The residual: anyone signed in can spend a domain's hourly budget by reloading a consent page. That delays only a client the domain hasn't registered yet, by up to an hour. Clients already provisioned keep serving their stored document.
4. **A per-person cap of 20 open-tier apps** (`Oauth::ClientMetadata::GRANT_CAP`).
   - It counts distinct open-tier clients the person holds a live grant to: unlapsed grants, as Connected apps lists them, delegated tokens excluded.
   - An app the person is already connected to is never refused, even past the cap, and a revoked or lapsed grant frees its place.
   - It refuses before any fetch, on the consent GET and the POST, with a 403 page that says what to do ("…Disconnect one in Connected apps to connect another"), not "unknown client". A denial is never capped.
   - Concurrent consents can over-admit by a handful, since nothing rechecks at grant creation. That's acceptable for a bound on rows.
5. **The FetchLease** (6 fetches in flight across processes), as before. It sits beside the fetcher's per-process bulkhead and 3-second deadline.

**Why no per-domain row quota.** The quota bounds one registrable domain. It doesn't bound someone using many, and public-suffix private entries (`*.vercel.app`, `*.pages.dev`, `*.netlify.app`, `*.workers.dev`, `user.github.io`) make domains free and plentiful. Each gets its own 25. Meanwhile it refuses a legitimate multi-tenant document host's 26th app silently, as an "unknown client", with nothing in telemetry to show it happened.

Together, the sweep and the cap bound what the quota was for:
- Unauthorized rows last a day, across every domain, which the quota never bounded.
- Rows that last are bounded per person, whatever domains they use.
- The shared domain budget bounds how fast any one domain adds clients.

**Why 20.** No account should approach it in normal use. While connecting apps is in preview, the most distinct third-party apps (dynamically registered or from a metadata document) any one person holds a live grant to is far below it. The preview's sample is small, so 20 is chosen for margin rather than fitted to it: several times what anyone uses, with room for someone who tries many agents. It's what bounds the permanent rows one account can hold.

## Refusal telemetry

Every refusal is logged and counted:
- Each one logs `[Oauth::ClientMetadata] refused reason=… tier=… domain=<registrable domain>`, plus the identity id for `grant_cap`.
- Each one is also reported as the OAuth event `oauth.client_metadata.refused` (`Oauth::Audit`), with reason, tier, registrable domain and identity. The SaaS engine writes it to the structured log, which matters because the hosted destinations turn plain log lines off. This is the evidence an operator reads to choose block-list entries.
- Each emits `cimd_refusal.oauth` with `reason` and `tier`. The SaaS engine counts it as `cimd_refusals_total{reason,tier}`, never labelled by domain.
- The reasons are `blocked_domain`, `budget` (a new client only; a provisioned client served from its stored document isn't refused), `grant_cap`, `lease` and `bulkhead`.
- Telemetry is best-effort and never costs the request its answer.

## Dark

Production changes nothing on landing. `OAUTH_CIMD_OPEN_REGISTRATION` is unset there, so:

- A host that isn't allowlisted is an unknown client before any lookup or fetch, as it is today, even when a row exists for it.
- Allowlisted hosts resolve as today, with the same per-person budget keys and limits.
- The fetch lease is off (`cimd_fetch_lease` follows open registration unless set).
- The block list is empty unless `OAUTH_CIMD_BLOCKED_DOMAINS` is set. Once set, it applies to the allowlisted tier too.

Some changes are live while dark, and all of them are benign:
- The new sweep step runs hourly. With the open tier dark there are no open-tier rows, save any left from a host taken off the allowlist, which can't resolve anyway.
- `cimd_fetches_total` and `cimd_clients_created_total{tier="recognized"}` start counting allowlisted fetches and registrations.

Dev and test turn the open tier on. beta1, the one destination besides production that sets `OAUTH_CIMD_ENABLED`, sets `OAUTH_CIMD_OPEN_REGISTRATION: "true"`. Light-up for production is a separate PR stacked on this one.

## What's ported

- **Tiers** (`Oauth::ClientMetadata.tier`): `:recognized` is an exact allowlisted host. Everything else, lookalikes like `claude.ai.example.com`, `evil-claude.ai` and case variants included, is `:open`. `registrable_domain` is bc3's (`PublicSuffix.domain`, with IP literal and case handling). `public_suffix` was only a transitive dependency, so it's now declared in the Gemfile.
- **Switch** (`Oauth::Availability.cimd_open_registration_enabled?`): fail-closed, and subordinate to `metadata_documents_enabled?`. When it's off, the open tier is refused before the row lookup. That's stricter than bc3, which lets established rows through.
- **FetchLease**: 6 fetches in flight, fail-fast and fail-closed, on both tiers. A slot is held for the budget check and the fetch, and released before the result is persisted.
  - MySQL: `GET_LOCK(name, 0)` and `RELEASE_LOCK`, on the connection the request holds.
  - SQLite: flock'd slot files beside the database.
  - Any other adapter, or any backend error, refuses.
- **Warnings**: the consent screen says "We don't know this app. Only authorize it if you trust `host`". Connected apps adds an "Unrecognized developer" note. Allowlisted hosts get neither.
- **Metrics**: `cimd_fetches_total{outcome}`, `cimd_lease_admissions_total{outcome}`, `cimd_lease_errors_total{operation}`, `cimd_clients_created_total{tier}` and `cimd_refusals_total{reason,tier}`. Labels come from fixed sets only.

## Left out, and departures from bc3

- **Device flow and PAR intake**: Fizzy has neither, so every open-tier row comes from a signed-in consent.
- **bc3's `disabled?` quarantine**: Fizzy clients have no disabled state. The block list covers incidents.
- **bc3's DomainQuota**: replaced as above. bc3 keeps its own.
- **Lease span**: bc3 persists inside the lease. Here the lease is released after the fetch, so database waits never hold a fetch slot.
- **Lock names** carry a digest of the database name as well as `Rails.env`.

## Tests

- **Resolver**:
  - the domain budget is shared across people, and a provisioned client resolves past a spent budget without counting a refusal;
  - the block list applies before any fetch, across hosts, in both tiers, to provisioned clients, at label boundaries and case-insensitively;
  - the grant cap refuses before any fetch, on read and intake, and refuses an app someone else provisioned;
  - the cap never refuses re-authorizing, counts only live open-tier grants (not lapsed, revoked, allowlisted, duplicate or someone else's), and leaves the recognized tier and denials alone;
  - each refusal reason is emitted with its tier, the log line names the domain, and a raising subscriber doesn't change the answer.
- **Client cleanup**:
  - an untouched open-tier client goes after a day, as do one consented to and never redeemed and one disconnected;
  - one used within a day, a granted one and an allowlisted one stay;
  - the locked recheck spares a client granted after it was picked.
- **Integration**:
  - an open-tier client consented to and never redeemed survives 23 hours, is swept at 25, and the next consent provisions it again and its code redeems;
  - someone at the cap gets the 403 page on GET and POST with no fetch, can still deny, and can still connect an allowlisted app;
  - a blocked domain is an unknown client, provisioned or not.
- **SaaS metrics**: `cimd_refusals_total` counts by reason and tier only.
- **Mutation check**: removing each new guard in turn fails at least one test. The guards are the sweep step, its tier filter, the shared budget key, the block check and its trailing-dot normalization, the cap's self-exclusion (also past the cap), the denial exemption, the live-grant filter, and the telemetry rescues.

Run on SQLite and on MySQL 8.4 (SaaS mode): the CIMD model, client, integration and SaaS metrics tests.

title: Open the metadata document open tier in production
Keep search words and what people write out of the logs
body:
Search words, and the text the API and the MCP server send, were written to the request log. This filters them the way bc3 does ([bc3 `config/initializers/filter_parameter_logging.rb`](https://github.com/basecamp/bc3/blob/95e272534fc3783b1e12aa313197a403dfb4aae4/config/initializers/filter_parameter_logging.rb#L59-L75): `q` exactly, `:query`, content fields).

## Fields filtered (`config/application.rb`)

| Field | Sent by |
|---|---|
| `q` (whole, at any depth) | search_cards, the search page |
| `terms` | list_cards |
| `title` (and `tag_title`) | create_card, update_card, tag_card |
| `description` (and `public_description`) | create_card, update_card, create_board, update_board |
| `body`, `content` | comments, steps, reactions |
| `name` | boards, columns, account settings, users |
| `email_address` | request_email_address_change |
| `timezone_name` | update_my_timezone |

These leave the Started line, the Parameters line, and the structured request line's URL and parameters. Because `filter_parameters` also feeds `filter_attributes`, SQLite's logged binds for those columns are masked too.

## Search words in SQL (`lib/rails_ext/active_record_sql_redaction.rb`)

Filtering `q` isn't enough on its own. MySQL runs without prepared statements, so the words are a literal in the search's `MATCH ... AGAINST`, and that statement is logged. The search index's own writes also carry the text of every card and comment they index. `search_records` joins the redacted tables. A suffix covers its 16 MySQL shards (`search_records_0`–`_15`) and SQLite's `search_records_fts`. `filters` joins them too: a saved filter keeps its search terms in `fields`, which MySQL inlines into the `INSERT`. The statement still reaches the database unchanged; only what's logged is redacted.

## Tests

`test/integration/content_parameter_logging_test.rb` captures everything a request logs at debug, SQL included:

- search (HTML and JSON) and list_cards' `terms`: neither the words nor their stem (what MySQL's `MATCH` carries) appear anywhere in the log, and the search's SQL is asserted present, so the absence check means something.
- a saved filter: its `INSERT` is logged without the terms, and the terms are stored.
- comment, card and step writes: the text is absent from the parameters and the request lines.
- every MCP field above is filtered, and lookalikes (`faq`, `qr`) stay visible.

With the redaction reverted, the two search tests fail. With the filter reverted, all four fail.

The existing control "statements against other tables keep their literals" looked up `identities.email_address`, which is now a filtered attribute. It uses a quoted literal on `cards.status` instead, which an over-reaching redaction would drop.

## Not in this PR

- **Content in other tables' SQL.** On MySQL, a card's title or a comment's body is still a literal in its own `INSERT`/`UPDATE` on `cards`, `action_text_rich_texts` or `steps`. Those tables' statements are the app's most common, and table-wide redaction drops everything after the first quote, ids included. Whether to redact them is a separate call.
- **Revoked-grant retention.** Fizzy has nothing to delete here: every way a grant ends destroys its row, so a revoked grant is gone at once.
  - Paths: `Identity::AccessToken#revoke` calls `destroy!` (`app/models/identity/access_token.rb:376-379`), used by Connected Apps, the revocation endpoint, My access tokens, the idle-lapse sweep and code replay. Client and identity deletion cascade with `dependent: :destroy`.
  - Fizzy's clocks against bc3's:
    - Delegated tokens: 1 hour past expiry, against bc3's 24 hours for access tokens.
    - Redeemed codes: 25 hours, against 24 hours past a 60-second code.
    - A grant idle 90 days lapses and is deleted within a day.
    - Retired refresh tokens: 90 days from rotation, against bc3's 7 days past a rotated token's own expiry (issue + 90 days). Matching bc3 exactly would need the retired token's issue time, which isn't stored.

Waiting on a person's word before merge.

title: Serve Muse's domain verification token on mcp.fizzy.do
body:
Muse's connector portal checks that we control `mcp.fizzy.do` by fetching `https://mcp.fizzy.do/.well-known/muse-challenge/<token>`. The pinned fizzy-mcp-server v0.2.8 serves the token when `FIZZY_MCP_MUSE_CHALLENGE` is set.

This sets it for production only, in clear env, since the token is public by design. It takes effect when the accessory restarts: `saas/bin/mcp-rolling-reboot production`.

title: Route hosted MCP to its own Kamal app in production and staging
body:
**Draft. Merge at the cutover, not before.** Running `saas/script/configure-lb-mcp.sh production` or `staging` from this branch is the cutover, and the hosts it names don't exist yet.

## What

`saas/script/configure-lb-mcp.sh` now points the load balancers' `fizzy_mcp` service at the hosted MCP server's own Kamal app (basecamp/fizzy-mcp-server, its `docs/operations/dedicated-deploy.md`) for production and staging:

| Destination | Targets | `--accessory` (rollback) |
|---|---|---|
| production | `fizzy-mcp-101`, `-102` (df-iad), `fizzy-mcp-01`, `-02` (sc-chi) | `fizzy-app-101`, `-102`, as now |
| staging | `fizzy-staging-mcp-101`, `fizzy-staging-mcp-01` | `fizzy-staging-app-101`, `-102`, as now |
| beta1 | `fizzy-beta-app-101`, as now | n/a |

Every target is now health-checked with the MCP host name (`--health-check-host`). kamal-proxy on the target routes by host. Without the flag, a dedicated host has nothing that answers the check, and an accessory host answers with the app's `/up`, which can't see the MCP container. With it, the check reaches the MCP server's own `/up` on both kinds of target. The balancers' `kamal-proxy deploy` waits for that check, so a target that doesn't answer keeps the old route.

`saas/bin/mcp-rolling-reboot` now refuses production and staging. Draining an accessory host there would move traffic to the dedicated hosts rather than drain it.

Nothing in front of the balancers changes: no F5 virtual server and no DNS.

## Cutover, per destination (staging first)

1. The hosts are provisioned, and basecamp/fizzy-mcp-server has deployed to them; its per-host canary passes.
2. `saas/script/configure-lb-mcp.sh <destination>` from this branch (or from `main`, once this is merged).
3. Verify `https://<mcp host>/up`, the protected-resource metadata, and that an unauthenticated `POST /mcp` gets a 401. Then sign in with a real client.

**Rollback:** `saas/script/configure-lb-mcp.sh <destination> --accessory`. Every balancer goes back to the accessory within seconds. This works until the accessory is removed (the follow-up draft).

## Checked

- `bash -n` passes. An unknown argument or destination is refused. `--without` refuses a host that isn't a target.
- With `ssh` stubbed, the generated `kamal-proxy deploy` lines for production, staging (dedicated and `--accessory`) and beta1 are as above, each with `--health-check-host`.
- I checked a health check with the MCP host name against today's accessory hosts (`curl -H 'Host: mcp.fizzy.do' http://localhost/up` on `fizzy-app-101` and `-102`). It answers 200 from the MCP server.

title: After cutover: remove the MCP accessory from production and staging
body:
**Draft, after cutover.** Land this only once production and staging are served by basecamp/fizzy-mcp-server's own Kamal app, and once `bin/kamal accessory remove fizzy_mcp -d <destination>` has run for each. It's stacked on #3339.

## What

- `saas/config/deploy.yml` now declares the `fizzy_mcp` accessory for the betas only. The production and staging files drop their `fizzy_mcp` blocks, along with staging's issuer TODO.
- `saas/.kamal/secrets.production` stops fetching `FIZZY_MCP_EXCHANGE_CLIENT_SECRET`, which the app never read. The stored secret stays, because the dedicated app reads it.
- `configure-lb-mcp.sh` drops `--accessory`, since there's no accessory left to route back to.
- `mcp-rolling-reboot` still refuses production and staging, now because they have no accessory.

This follows bc3's removal of `basecamp_mcp` for production and staging, which kept the betas.

## Order

1. Cut over a destination (#3339) and verify it.
2. `bin/kamal accessory remove fizzy_mcp -d staging`, then the same with `-d production`. Do this before merging: once this lands, Kamal no longer knows the accessory for those destinations.
3. Merge this.

Rollback after step 2: boot the accessory again from a commit before this one (`bin/kamal accessory boot fizzy_mcp -d <destination>`), then run that commit's `configure-lb-mcp.sh <destination> --accessory`.

## Checked

I rendered the Kamal config through `Kamal::Configuration` for each destination, before and after this change:

| Destination | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| production | hotcell, fizzy_mcp, load-balancer | hotcell, load-balancer |
| staging | hotcell, fizzy_mcp, load-balancer | hotcell, load-balancer |
| beta1 | hotcell, fizzy_mcp, load-balancer | unchanged |

The production and staging files parse.

title: Keep the email change confirmation token out of the job log
body:
The email change confirmation token was being logged: it was passed to `UserMailer.email_change_confirmation` as a `deliver_later` argument, so Active Job wrote it into its enqueue and perform log lines, and into the job row.

It no longer is. The mailer now takes the user, the address the change was requested from and the new address, and generates the token itself, the way `Notification::BundleMailer` generates its unsubscribe token, so the token never enters the job's arguments. No logging configuration changes.

- `User#email_address_change_token(from:, to:)` generates the token, with the 30-minute expiry kept in the model.
- The token is now generated when the mail is delivered rather than when the change is requested, so its 30 minutes run from delivery. It stays bound to the address the change was requested from, so a confirmation delivered after another change has landed doesn't confirm.
- A confirmation mail enqueued by the old code during the deploy will fail on the new mailer signature; requesting the change again sends a new one.

The new test performs the mail delivery job with Active Job's log captured, takes the token from the delivered mail's link, and checks it is absent from the log and still confirms the change. It fails on the previous code, where the token appears on both the enqueue and perform lines. A second test changes the address between enqueue and delivery and checks the delivered token no longer confirms.

The other mailers and jobs pass records rather than tokens or codes. The magic link mailer passes the `MagicLink` record and the bundle mailer generates its unsubscribe token itself, and the native push job already turns off argument logging.

title: Let Muse connect to the Fizzy MCP as a recognized app by its metadata document
body:
Muse's MCP connector identifies by its Client ID Metadata Document, `https://platform.muse.ai/oauth/client-metadata.json`. `platform.muse.ai` isn't a recognized CIMD host. Where open registration is on, Muse reaches consent only through the open tier: consent and Connected apps warn that we don't know the app, it counts toward the per-person cap on open-tier apps, and its client is swept with the open tier's. Where it's off, Muse is refused as an unknown client.

- Adds `platform.muse.ai` to `OAUTH_CIMD_ALLOWED_HOSTS` in `saas/config/deploy.yml`, and to the development and test lists, so Muse is a recognized app. Exact host match as before: `muse.ai`, `evil.platform.muse.ai` and `platform.muse.ai.example.com` stay unrecognized (`url_test.rb`).
- The fixture is Muse's published document as of 2026-11-25. It names no `scope`, so it's provisioned with read and write, and its `none` auth method, `authorization_code` grant and one https callback pass `Oauth::ClientMetadata::Document`. The new integration test carries it through consent and token exchange on its `platform.muse.ai` callback, with no unknown-app warning on consent and a provisioned client that isn't open tier. Without the host change that test fails on the warning.
- `saas/test/lib/oauth_cimd_allowed_hosts_test.rb` now also asserts production's deploy list includes `platform.muse.ai`.

Personal data: no new service on our side. Muse receives a token only when someone connects it and approves consent, as with Claude, ChatGPT and Perplexity.

title: Serve OpenAI's domain verification token from the Fizzy MCP accessory
body:
OpenAI's Fizzy plugin draft checks `https://mcp.fizzy.do/.well-known/openai-apps-challenge` for its token before it connects the server for review. fizzy-mcp-server serves `FIZZY_MCP_OPENAI_APPS_CHALLENGE` there when it's set, and this sets it on the production `fizzy_mcp` accessory, beside the Muse token from #3338.

The token is public by design. Deploy-config only; it takes effect on `saas/bin/mcp-rolling-reboot production`.

title: Set no form-action on the consent screen
body:
OpenAI's plugin dashboard now connects by CIMD as `https://chatgpt.com/oauth/client.json`, with redirect_uri `https://chatgpt.com/connector_platform_oauth_redirect`, which redirects on to `platform.openai.com`. Browsers apply CSP `form-action` to every hop of a form submission. The consent screen allowed only the validated redirect origin, so it blocked the second hop: Authorize and Deny answered 302 and the page never moved (the Fizzy plugin draft's Connect step, 2026-11-25). Before CIMD the dashboard registered by DCR with a platform.openai.com callback, which is why it worked earlier.

Any legitimate client's redirect target may redirect on, and no list of origins can name every next hop, so the consent controller now sets no `form-action` (Jeremy's call). The per-request origin computation (`validated_redirect_form_action_source` and its patterns) is removed. Every other page keeps the app-wide `form-action 'self'`, and the consent page still does a full load, so it never inherits that one by Turbo.

- Tests: the consent screen (GET) and its POST answer carry no form-action; another page keeps `'self'`. The old per-origin form-action tests are replaced.
- `bin/rails test test/integration/oauth_*.rb test/integration/static_csp_test.rb`: 455 tests, 0 failures.
- `test/system/oauth_consent_test.rb` errors locally with Chrome 158's "* is not a valid URL" in Selenium, on unchanged main too.

title: Pin fizzy-mcp-server v0.2.9
body:
The `fizzy_mcp` accessory boots v0.2.9 by digest, as `scripts/build-image.sh` printed it from the cosign-verified release: `update_board_entropy` is served as `update_board_auto_postpone`, the name OpenAI's plugin scan asked for (basecamp/fizzy-mcp-server#55). Rollback re-pins v0.2.8.

title: Bump puma from 8.0.4 to 8.1.2
body:
Bumps [puma](https://github.com/puma/puma) from 8.0.4 to 8.1.2.
Release notes

Sourced from puma's releases.

v8.1.2

  • Security
    • Close a TLS connection when OpenSSL reports a fatal error reading it, rather than buffering everything the client sends until first_data_timeout. (GHSA-4v6q-hvv7-49h9)
    • On JRuby, stop request headers such as Query-String and Request-Path from changing QUERY_STRING, PATH_INFO and the other env keys that come from the request line. (GHSA-rhww-p99c-hgj9)

CVE IDs have been requested for these advisories and will be added here once assigned.

v8.1.1

  • Bugfixes
    • Fix pumactl stop and SIGINT hanging in cluster mode when an after_stopped hook owns child processes (#4135)
    • Fix TLS stream corruption on TruffleRuby when flushing to a full socket (#4108)
    • Stop shipping development-only files in the gem (#4124)

  • Features

title: Bump zip_kit from 6.4.1 to 6.4.3
body:
Bumps [zip_kit](https://github.com/julik/zip_kit) from 6.4.1 to 6.4.3.
Changelog

Sourced from zip_kit's changelog.

6.4.3

  • Move the test suite from RSpec to minitest and run it in parallel, in one forked process per CPU core. Run it with bundle exec rake test (it was rake spec), and see CONTRIBUTING.md for TEST_WORKERS and SEED. The rspec, rspec-mocks and complexity_assert development dependencies are gone. Nothing changes for users of the library.
  • Make FileReader.read_zip_structure check the offset and size of the Zip64 end of central directory record against the position of the Zip64 EOCD locator, and raise FileReader::InvalidStructure if the record does not fit in front of it. The 8-byte record size went straight into IO#read, and File#read allocates the requested length upfront - so a crafted archive made reading it raise NoMemoryError, which rescue => e does not catch. Over RemoteIO it fetched the rest of the object instead. (#41)
  • Raise FileReader::ReadError instead of RangeError when an offset in the archive is too large to seek to, like a Zip64 local header offset of 2**64 - 1. (#42)
  • Raise FileReader::MissingEOCD when FileReader.read_zip_structure is given an empty IO. It raised a NoMethodError (undefined method 'bytesize' for nil) before, which callers could not rescue as a ZIP error. (#38)
  • Make FileReader.read_zip_structure read at most the declared central directory size (plus 64KB of allowance for archives which misreport it), instead of everything from the start of the central directory to the end of the IO. An archive with data stuffed in front of the EOCD made the reader load all of it into one String - over RemoteIO, download all of it. A central directory offset past the EOCD now raises FileReader::InvalidStructure. (#39)
  • Make the reader returned by ZipEntry#extractor_from raise FileReader::InvalidStructure once a deflated entry inflates to more than its declared uncompressed size, instead of returning whatever the deflate stream produces. Inflation now happens in 16KB pieces, so a single extract call no longer inflates a small chunk of input into many megabytes before returning. (#40)

6.4.2

  • Write every ZIP record with a single Array#pack and a single << to the destination, instead of one per field. Archives with lots of entries get written about 1.5x faster.
  • Unpack the fixed fields of local and central directory headers in one go in FileReader, and read 4KB upfront for a local file header instead of the maximum possible 128KB. FileReader.read_zip_structure with local headers gets about 5x faster on archives with many entries, and parsing the central directory alone about 2x.
  • Fix ZipWriter converting the given mtime to UTC in place. The local file header got the DOS time in local time and the central directory header got it in UTC, and the caller was left with a Time object in UTC.
  • Remove the C_CHAR and C_INT4 constants from ZipWriter, which were never meant to be public (the other packspec constants were private already).
  • Add "cache-control" => "no-transform" to OutputEnumerator.streaming_http_headers, and add no-transform to the Cache-Control of the response in zip_kit_stream (keeping whatever the controller has set there). Rack::Deflater only leaves a response alone if it has no-transform or a content encoding other than identity, so the content-encoding: identity we were sending did not stop it - it gzipped the ZIP all the same, and with sync: false buffered all of it to do so. If you replace our cache-control with your own, keep no-transform in it.
